title_page_text: CASE STUDY: DEEMOUTH ARTIST STUDIOS AND EDIT ABERDEEN
The Visible Value of the Invisible Workforce
Overview

Deemouth Artist Studios (DAST), based at the Deemouth Business Centre in Torry, Aberdeen, is one of the clearest illustrations in this research of the gap between what official statistics record and what is actually happening in the regional creative economy. It is a working community of artists, designers, makers and craftspeople - potters, painters, sculptors, upholsterers, jewellers, ceramicists - operating at the intersection of professional practice, community enterprise and cultural infrastructure. None of them appear in the Business Register and Employment Survey. Very few have a LinkedIn profile. By every conventional measure of economic activity, they are invisible. And yet, as this case study demonstrates, they are generating real commercial revenue, sustaining a retail presence in Aberdeen city centre, attracting footfall to a struggling shopping centre, and providing the kind of authentic, place-rooted cultural offer that no amount of digital investment can replicate.

DAST was founded and is managed by Peter Baxter and Allan Watson. Baxter's background is in accountancy and plumbing; he came to the creative sector not through artistic training but through a conviction that talented people deserve the infrastructure to earn from their work. That pragmatic, commercially-minded approach to supporting creative practice is reflected in DAST. It is not a subsidised arts project; it is a community of practice with a retail arm, a training function, a fabrication and exhibition support service, and a growing relationship with the higher education sector. It is, in the language of this report, a Tier 4 organisation that is actively converting invisible creative capacity into visible economic value.
The Community: Who Is in Tier 4?

The DAST community illustrates the diversity and complexity of the Tier 4 population. Baxter describes a membership that ranges from "ladies that paint" through to "serious trading people that deal with five-star hotels and whisky companies and go to Goldsmiths and sell commercially as well."
This is not a homogeneous group. It includes:
Practitioners for whom creative work is their primary professional activity and principal source of income, operating at a fully commercial level with established wholesale and retail relationships.
Practitioners for whom creative work is one component of a portfolio of activities: part-time professional practice combined with teaching, community work, or other employment.

Practitioners for whom creative work is a serious vocation rather than a primary income source, but whose output is of genuine commercial quality and whose participation in the creative economy is real and sustained.

The Tier 4 population is not a single category of "hobbyists" or "amateurs." It is a spectrum of engagement with creative practice, ranging from the fully professional to the seriously committed non-professional, and the economic contribution of each point on that spectrum is real, if variable. The DAST community also includes the Aberdeen Ceramic School, a trading entity offering both school facilities and membership, and an upholstery school whose operator both trades and teaches. These are not peripheral activities. They are small businesses generating revenue, providing skills training, and contributing to the cultural life of the city.
Edit Aberdeen Retail Outlet: Making the Invisible Visible

The most significant commercial development associated with DAST is the establishment of Edit Aberdeen, a retail outlet in the Bon Accord Centre in Aberdeen city centre. Edit began as a retail platform for DAST members but has since broadened to include makers from across Aberdeenshire, reflecting the wider distributed creative economy of the region.

Edit is constituted as a Community Interest Company. Its presence in the Bon Accord Centre is supported by Robert Gordon University's Gray's School of Art, which acts as a charitable backer, enabling Edit to occupy commercial retail space at zero business rates under the provisions that apply to charitable occupiers of otherwise empty commercial lots. This is a practical and effective model of creative economy support that could be more widely adopted in economic development and regeneration frameworks.

In the year prior to this research, Edit generated £100,000 in retail sales for the artists and makers whose work it stocks. Of that revenue, 60% is returned directly to the makers; 40% is retained by Edit to sustain its operations and is reinvested in the infrastructure that makes the next £100,000 possible.

These figures are not captured anywhere in official economic statistics. The makers whose work sells through Edit are not registered as businesses in the conventional sense. Their income does not appear in BRES. Their activity does not generate a Companies House filing. They are, in the precise sense used in this report, part of the Tier 4 invisible workforce.
The Retail Economy Effect: Creative Presence as Commercial Catalyst

One of the most striking observations in Baxter's account of Edit's development concerns its effect on the surrounding retail environment. Since Edit opened in the Bon Accord Centre, a cluster of aspirational retail brands has appeared in its immediate vicinity, including Sostrene Grene, Fat Face and Superdry. Peter Baxter is explicit that he did not approach these brands or negotiate their arrival; they came because they recognised what Edit was bringing to that part of the centre.

This is a textbook illustration of an agglomeration effect that is rarely captured in economic impact assessments. A curated, well-merchandised retail outlet, managed by Jo, a DAST resident who previously worked in merchandising for John Lewis, creates a quality signal that attracts complementary commercial activity. The creative economy does not just generate its own direct economic value; it creates the conditions in which other economic activity becomes viable.

This effect is directly relevant to the strategic argument of this report. The Bon Accord Centre, like the Trinity Centre and other parts of Aberdeen city centre, has been struggling with vacancy and footfall. Edit's presence has contributed to reversing that trend in its immediate vicinity. The cost to the public purse of that contribution is, in effect, zero: the charitable rate relief model means that Edit occupies its space without displacing a rate-paying tenant, and the footfall it generates benefits the centre as a whole.
The University Relationship: Pipeline and Partnership

The DAST and Edit ecosystem has developed a significant and mutually beneficial relationship with Robert Gordon University's Gray's School of Art that is not visible in any formal partnership agreement or institutional record, but that is generating real educational and economic value.

Third and fourth year cohorts from Gray's School of Art now interact directly with Edit as part of their professional development. A recent cohort in three-dimensional design completed a ten-week course focused on developing a product that is commercially scalable, reflects the history and identity of Aberdeen, and is suitable for retail through Edit. These are live commercial briefs with a real retail outlet as their destination. Students who engage with Edit leave with a product in a shop, a retail relationship, and a practical understanding of the commercial creative economy.

This relationship illustrates one of the central arguments of this report about the graduate retention crisis. The students who engage with Edit through their coursework are not just learning about the creative economy in the abstract; they are becoming part of it. They are building relationships with practitioners, developing products for a real market, and experiencing the possibility of a creative career in Aberdeen that does not require them to move to Edinburgh or London to find an audience for their work. The economic value of that graduate retention to the region is difficult to quantify precisely, but it is real and it is significant.

Baxter also notes that this relationship emerged organically, without formal institutional promotion. When the research team spoke with RGU about its engagement with the creative economy, the conversation focused on student recruitment and destinations and did not touch on the kind of live commercial partnerships that the Edit relationship represents. This is an example of a systemic gap in how the creative economy is understood and communicated by the institutions that are most deeply embedded in it.
The Broader Ecosystem: Open Studios, NEOS and the Concentric Circles of Creative Practice

DAST and Edit do not exist in isolation. They are part of a broader ecosystem of creative practice in Aberdeen and Aberdeenshire that includes the North East Open Studios (NEOS) programme, Craig's Mobile Art School, and a range of community and heritage organisations across the region.

The relationship between DAST's membership and NEOS participation is analytically important for this report. Understanding the extent to which the DAST community overlaps with and participates in NEOS is essential to avoiding double-counting in the Tier 4 estimate. Baxter's description of the DAST community, which includes practitioners at every point on the spectrum from serious commercial trading to occasional creative practice, suggests that the overlap is real but partial: some DAST members participate in NEOS, others do not, and the NEOS participant population extends well beyond the DAST community into the wider distributed creative economy of Aberdeenshire.

This series of "concentric circles", with DAST at the centre, Edit as the commercial interface, NEOS as the wider network, and the rural and coastal dispersal of individual practitioners beyond that, is precisely the kind of ecosystem that is missed by conventional economic measurement. It has no single legal entity, no consolidated accounts, no employer registration. It is held together by relationships, shared spaces, informal networks and a common commitment to making creative practice economically viable in a city that has not always recognised its value.

title_page_text: PLAIN ENGLISH SUMMARY
The Creative Industries in Aberdeen and Aberdeenshire: What We Found and Why It Matters
What This Research Is About

This report maps the creative industries in Aberdeen City and Aberdeenshire – the businesses, freelancers, artists, makers, designers, musicians, architects, filmmakers and technologists who make up the region's creative economy. It draws on official employment data, analysis of over 9,400 LinkedIn profiles, real-time business intelligence from The Data City platform, and direct consultation with practitioners and stakeholders across four in-person workshops and a series of other individual and group calls.

The research was commissioned to provide a robust evidence base for the Regional Economic Strategy and to support the case for investment in the creative sector as part of the region's transition away from dependence on oil and gas.
What We Found: The Creative Economy Is Bigger Than It Looks

Official employment figures – based on government surveys of businesses registered for payroll tax – record around 3,300 people working in the creative industries in Aberdeen and Aberdeenshire. But this significantly understates the true picture.

When we look at LinkedIn profiles, we find over 5,400 people in the region with creative occupations, roughly half of whom are freelancers, self-employed practitioners, or contractors who would not appear in official employment statistics. Add to this the artists, makers, musicians and craftspeople who have little or no digital presence – working from home studios, shared workshops, and rural spaces across Aberdeenshire – and the total creative workforce is closer to 7,500 people.

Together, these practitioners generate an estimated £315 million in direct economic value each year, rising to £474 million when the knock-on effects through supply chains and local spending are taken into account.
The Structure of the Creative Workforce
The creative workforce in Aberdeen and Aberdeenshire is not a single, uniform group. It is made up of four distinct layers, each with different characteristics and different needs:

Tier 1: Large cultural institutions - museums, libraries, Aberdeen Performing Arts and similar organisations – provide the visible public face of the creative sector and employ around 1,180 people, many of them part-time. They are stable anchors for the wider ecosystem but have limited capacity for rapid growth.

Tier 2: Creative businesses – the architects, designers, advertising agencies, software developers, filmmakers and other commercial firms that make up the productive core of the sector – employ around 2,125 people, mostly full-time. Architecture is a particular strength, with around 400 staff and a strong track record linked to the region's built environment and energy sector. A cluster of high-value creative technology firms – in software, games, film and video production – represents the sector's productivity engine, generating significantly more economic value per person than the creative sector average.

Tier 3: Freelancers and independent professionals – around 2,370 people who work on a project-by-project basis, offering skills in marketing, design, film production, photography, publishing and creative technology. This group is essential to the commercial creative economy: it provides the flexible, specialist capacity that allows businesses to take on new projects without the risk of permanent hiring. It is also the layer most likely to bring new skills and ideas into the region, and the one most at risk of being overlooked in policy.

Tier 4: The invisible cultural workforce – an estimated 1,855 practitioners, including professional artists, makers, musicians and craftspeople, who work largely outside formal employment structures and have little or no presence on digital platforms. Many are based in Aberdeenshire, working from home studios, converted farm buildings and shared spaces. They are not captured by official statistics, but they are a real and economically significant part of the creative economy.
The Central Challenge: A Fragmented Sector That Doesn't Know Its Own Strength

The single most consistent message from our consultation with practitioners (which resulted in over 1,100 separate information points and insights) was that the creative sector in Aberdeen and Aberdeenshire feels hidden, undervalued and disconnected; not because the work isn't happening, but because it isn't visible, either to the outside world or to practitioners themselves.

The region has a cultural habit of understatement. People here are reluctant to talk up their own work, even when it is objectively excellent. This is not false modesty; it is a deeply ingrained regional characteristic. But in a competitive creative economy, where reputation, visibility and self-advocacy are essential tools, it becomes a strategic liability.

At the same time, the sector is structurally fragmented. Subsectors – film, design, music, craft, architecture, games – operate largely in parallel, with limited interaction. The freelance workforce, which should be the connective tissue linking these communities, is instead dispersed and under-supported. Businesses are locked into familiar client relationships, primarily with the energy sector, and struggle to see opportunities in adjacent markets.

The result is a sector that is training talented people and then watching them leave – not because there is no work here, but because the structures that would allow them to find it, build on it, and stay are not yet in place.
The Opportunity: Why Now, and Why Here

The region's dependence on oil and gas is both its greatest challenge and its greatest opportunity. The energy transition is already underway, and it is creating real demand for skills that the creative sector is well placed to supply: data visualisation, technical storytelling, simulation, digital communication, and the ability to explain complex change to diverse audiences.

Aberdeen and Aberdeenshire have specific advantages that are easy to overlook. The cost of living and working here is significantly lower than in London, Edinburgh or Glasgow. The quality of life – landscape, community, space – is a genuine draw for people who want to build a sustainable creative practice rather than a high-pressure urban career. The region has a deep well of authentic experience of industrial transition, boom and bust, and community resilience that gives its creative practitioners a distinctive voice and perspective.

There are already signs of what is possible when the conditions are right. A small animation cluster has emerged organically in Aberdeen, bringing together practitioners who recognised shared interests and began collaborating. This happened without a formal programme or significant public investment. It is an example of what the research calls a "constellation": a node of creative collaboration that emerges when people with complementary skills find each other and a reason to work together.

The question is not whether Aberdeen and Aberdeenshire can build a stronger creative economy. The evidence shows clearly that the foundations are already there. The question is whether the conditions can be created, through investment, policy, skills development, and a stronger shared narrative, to allow more of these constellations to form and to grow.
What Needs to Happen
The research points to three interconnected priorities:

First, make the sector visible. The creative economy in Aberdeen and Aberdeenshire is significantly larger and more economically significant than official data suggests. Making this case clearly, consistently and in plain terms, to Scottish Government, to investors, to other sectors of the economy, and to practitioners themselves, is a precondition for everything else. The evidence base now exists to do this.

Second, invest in the connective tissue. The freelance workforce is not a problem to be solved; it is the region's most valuable source of creative agility and cross-sector knowledge transfer. Supporting it through shared infrastructure, professional development, market access, and peer networks will do more to strengthen the creative economy than any number of new buildings or formal programmes.

Third, align skills with demand. The region is training creative graduates who then leave, not because there are no opportunities here, but because the local economy has not yet developed the absorption capacity to make use of their skills. Addressing this requires investment in creative supply chains and business development, not just in training. It also requires a more honest conversation between universities, colleges, employers and practitioners about what skills are actually needed and what career pathways are genuinely available.

title_page_text: Creative industries in North East Scotland: evidence, analysis and strategic priorities
Executive summary
What this document is and who it is for

Aberdeen and Aberdeenshire hold an unusual position in the national creative economy. A concentration of simulation capability at four times the UK average, generated through fifty years of offshore energy operations, sits alongside a cultural ecosystem whose anchor organisations, graduate pipeline and freelance practitioner base are substantially larger and more productive than any previous policy account has recognised. The convergence between these two formations is already generating new institutions, new commercial activity and new research territory. Further policy support and systematic measurement and dissemination of that capability is needed to ensure that the creative economy fulfils both economic and societal needs.

This executive summary presents the principal findings of a comprehensive assessment of that economy. It is addressed at once to Regional Economic Partnership members and local authority decision-makers; to practitioners and organisations working across the creative, cultural and digital sectors; and to any reader with an interest in how the North East of Scotland positions itself for sustained economic growth during a period of rapid structural change.

It draws on original analysis combining official government data, real-time company intelligence and workforce profiling with stakeholder consultation and comparative research. It makes the case for strategic investment grounded in evidence. It identifies specific funding opportunities and policy levers that are available now. And it charts the growth pathways available at each level of a creative economy that is larger, more productive and more strategically distinctive than any previous account has recognised.
Why previous accounts of this economy have been incomplete

Standard approaches to measuring creative industries rely on two official data sources: the Business Register and Employment Survey (BRES), which counts formally employed workers in registered businesses; and the Inter-Departmental Business Register (IDBR), which records companies by their declared Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) code, the official system used to categorise companies by their declared business activity at the point of registration. Both are authoritative but both systematically undercount the creative economy in Aberdeen and Aberdeenshire.

BRES misses the large population of self-employed and freelance practitioners who are neither employed by a firm nor registered as an employer themselves. In a sector where over 90% of enterprises employ fewer than ten people and where many practitioners operate through portfolio working, part-time activity and informal contracts, this is not a marginal omission. It is the difference between a partial and a complete picture.

SIC codes present a different but equally significant problem. They record what a company declares itself to be at the point of registration, not what it actually does. In the North East, a substantial population of firms in the energy, subsea and engineering sectors routinely uses creative-origin technical skills, including real-time three-dimensional visualisation, simulation, digital twin development and immersive content production, as a core part of its commercial offer. Under standard SIC classification, only a minority of these firms appears in creative industries counts. Their exclusion is the single largest source of systematic error in previous estimates of the regional creative economy.

A third limitation is specific to this region. The IT consultancy sector (SIC 62.02) accounts for substantial employment and an estimated £150m in gross value added (GVA). Detailed sector intelligence and stakeholder consultation confirm that this activity functions primarily as enterprise support for the energy sector rather than as creative production. Including it would inflate the creative economy count while misrepresenting its character. This report separates measurement of IT consultancy from the strategic creative core, with a methodological crosswalk retained to allow comparison with headline national figures.
How the creative economy was measured

Arriving at an accurate account required working across three distinct layers of evidence and reconciling them through a sequence of analytical steps designed to avoid both double-counting and systematic exclusion.

The first layer is the official baseline. BRES data for Aberdeen City and Aberdeenshire, filtered against creative industries SIC codes and adjusted to remove general IT consultancy, produces an employment count of some 3,300 workers. This is the floor of the analysis: the population whose economic activity is formally registered, reliably counted and analytically secure. It captures the region’s publicly funded cultural institutions, its registered design and architecture practices, and its commercial creative firms. It does not capture freelancers, sole traders or the convergence of the digital and creative economies.

The second layer draws on two proprietary real-time sources. The Data CityTM platform analyses company website content to assign Real-Time Industrial Classifications (RTICs), descriptions of what firms actually do rather than how they are officially classified. This identified a broader population of active firms than official records alone, particularly in Createch (creative technology: firms applying creative methods to digital and technological products and services), video production and digital agency sectors, along with a cohort of businesses active in the region but registered elsewhere. Results were subject to human validation to confirm operational presence in the region and to identify subsidiaries of larger organisations. LinkedIn analysis, treating the platform as a large pre-filled workforce survey rather than a social media tool, identified some 9,400 unique profiles of North East residents with creative sector occupations. After removing enterprise IT profiles, the remaining 5,400-plus provided evidence of a workforce split broadly evenly between employed and independent practitioners, with over 2,350 additional creative workers not captured in official employment statistics.

The third layer is sector intelligence: qualitative and quantitative validation through stakeholder workshops, industry consultation and review of comparable studies from other regions, including the Liverpool Music Futures cluster mapping study (2026) whose methodology informed the treatment of shared utility employment in the live music and events economy. This layer validates quantitative findings against the lived experience of practitioners and employers, and identifies patterns of portfolio working, part-time practice and informal creative-industrial collaboration that quantitative sources cannot fully capture.

From this triangulation, the analysis constructs a four-tier model of the strategic creative core accounting for a total creative workforce of some 7,500 people. GVA estimates are derived from ONS regional output data apportioned to SIC codes on the basis of official employment, benchmarked against sector averages from Data City company records and DCMS economic estimates, and adjusted for the full-time equivalent (FTE) intensity that characterises each tier’s employment structure. Total economic impact is then calculated by applying Type II multipliers to each tier’s direct GVA figure. The multipliers applied at each tier reflect its distinct economic character, as described below.
The economy in four tiers: what the data shows and what it means
Tier 1: institutional anchors

Identified through BRES and IDBR and confirmed against Creative Scotland funding records, Tier 1 comprises publicly funded cultural institutions, museums, libraries and major performing arts venues. It accounts for some 1,180 workers (807 FTE, reflecting the high incidence of part-time, casual and sessional working common in event-led cultural organisations) and direct GVA of £19m. A Type II multiplier of 1.40, reflecting stable but restricted public procurement supply chains, produces a total economic impact of £26m.

The modest direct GVA contribution of Tier 1 can be misleading. These organisations,  which include Aberdeen Performing Arts, Peacock Visual Arts, the region’s museum and library infrastructure and the professional anchor organisations of the Aberdeenshire cultural ecosystem, are not primarily productivity generators. They are economic and social infrastructure: sustaining the audience relationships, graduate placements and professional development pathways that the commercial tiers depend on, and holding the institutional knowledge of a creative ecology whose depth is measured in decades rather than funding cycles.
Tier 2: the SME commercial core

Identified primarily through BRES/IDBR and augmented by Data City RTIC analysis, particularly in Createch, video production and digital agency sectors, Tier 2 comprises registered businesses in all parts of the creative industries, including architecture, design, advertising, film, television and video production, publishing, music, visual and performing arts and creative software. It accounts for some 2,125 workers, which equates to 1,934 FTE, reflecting high levels of full-time employment, and generates direct GVA of £190m. A Type II multiplier of 1.60, reflecting the extensive supply chain activity of commercial firms including rent, services and equipment expenditure, produces a total economic impact of £305m.

Two sub-sectors within Tier 2 are of particular strategic significance. Architecture and the built environment, employing around 400 staff at high FTE intensity, reflects a historical strength sustained by the region’s energy legacy and supported by new capital projects in renewable energy. The Createch sub-sector, which becomes analytically visible only once general IT consultancy is excluded from the count, comprises a robust cluster of high-value creative software, film, television, video and gaming firms whose GVA per head is markedly higher than the sector average. This is the region’s creative productivity engine and the tier most directly relevant to the “convergence economy” argument developed below.
Tier 3: visible freelancers

Identified through verified LinkedIn data, Tier 3 comprises independent professionals, describing themselves as freelance, self-employed or contractors, working across advertising, marketing, film, television and video production, games development, photography, publishing and Createch. LinkedIn provides a second source to verify the statistical evidence of employment from BRES and identifies a further 2,370 individual subscriber accounts (1,778 FTE) of freelance, self-employed and contract workers who collectively generate direct GVA of £80m. A Type II multiplier of 1.40, driven by local consumption of earnings rather than supply chain spend, produces a total economic impact of £111m.

This tier performs a function that GVA figures alone do not convey. It provides the flexible, skilled capacity that allows commercial firms in Tier 2 to scale rapidly in response to project opportunities without carrying permanent overhead. In a sector characterised by short-term commissions and variable demand, a deep and visible freelance pool is a structural competitive advantage. It is also the tier most directly affected by the graduate retention challenge: at present, only 17% of graduates from Aberdeen and Aberdeenshire’s higher education institutions remain employed in the region after completing their studies, and many of those who do stay enter Tier 3 practice in ways that make them invisible to official counts, with the consequence that their contribution goes unmeasured.
Tier 4: the invisible workforce

Tier 4 cannot be measured directly. It is inferred from penetration gap analysis: the difference between the estimated total population of creative practitioners in low-digital sub-sectors — including professional artists, makers, musicians and craft practitioners — and the proportion of that population identifiable through LinkedIn and official data. Independent musicians, artists, writers and craft makers show LinkedIn penetration rates estimated at between 30% and 45%, compared with over 80% for technology and design professionals. The scale of this tier, some 1,855 individuals (835 FTE), is derived from comparison with the Liverpool Music Futures cluster mapping study and validated through workshop feedback. A further 180 FTE of shared utility employment, hospitality and events staff facilitating the live music and events economy, is attributed to this tier using the same methodology.
Direct GVA is estimated at £27m, with a Type II multiplier of 1.20 reflecting lower disposable income and more limited supply chain activity, producing a total economic impact of £32m.

Executive Summary

Aberdeen’s creative economy is not a cultural peripheral; it is a £415 million industrial engine that is 2.7 times larger than official statistics record and currently serves as the primary absorptive pool for the region’s displaced high-skill technical labour [4]. While official Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) data captures only 3,305 employees, workforce mapping reveals a true population of 9,190 individuals generating high-value output at the intersection of energy services and digital technology [1]. This discrepancy is not a matter of minor mismeasurement; it is a structural "Classification Chasm" that leaves the city’s most significant competitive advantage—a concentration of simulation and visualisation skills 6.4 times the UK per capita average—ineligible for the very creative and innovation funding designed to support regional diversification [4].

The evidence indicates that Aberdeen is currently experiencing a profound "Scissors Effect." The region has recorded the sharpest job contraction in the UK over the last decade, with employment falling by 11.3% between 2013 and 2023 [4]. Simultaneously, however, the city has maintained the 5th most highly qualified workforce in the country, with 62.4% of the population holding high-level qualifications [4]. This surplus of technical talent is not leaving the region in the volumes expected; instead, it is migrating into a "Convergence Tier" of 218 firms. These companies, often registered under "Technical Testing" or "Engineering" codes to satisfy energy supply chain procurement, are effectively a dark matter creative sector. They provide the digital twins, VR safety environments, and subsea visualisations essential for the North Sea’s decommissioning and net-zero transition, yet they sit outside the remit of both Skills Development Scotland’s creative assessments and Creative Scotland’s cultural funding.

Beyond this high-tech tier lies a second, equally invisible substrate of approximately 1,855 independent and community practitioners [1]. While documented in local research as far back as 2014, this cohort remains absent from the formal economic frameworks that dictate regional skills investment. This group provides the cultural stickiness required to retain the 15% of the population currently in their 30s—the highest percentage in Scotland [5]. If this independent base remains unsupported, Aberdeen risks a talent evaporation event where the human capital required to sustain the Convergence Tier migrates to established creative hubs like Dundee or Edinburgh, where policy legibility is higher.
The following findings define the current strategic reality:

The Simulation Outlier: Aberdeen’s density of simulation and visualisation capability (6.4x UK average) is a global anomaly, comparable to Tier-1 creative tech hubs like Montreal or Bristol [4]. This is a defensible physical world moat that generic AI cannot easily displace due to the requirement for deep energy domain knowledge.

The GVA Paradox: The mapped creative economy contributes approximately 4% of Aberdeen’s total GVA (£415m of £10.3bn), yet receives less than 1.2% of targeted economic development support when place-making and festivals are excluded [4, 8].

The Skills-Policy Lag: Formal education pipelines in the region face a "Curriculum Design Lag" of 36–48 months, while the industrial simulation market operates on 18-month technical cycles. This forces firms to rely on informal, peer-to-peer training networks that are 100–500 times more cost-effective but entirely unrecognised by national skills funding [1].

The Acquisition Risk: Within a 24-36 month window, the lack of regional connective tissue and sector-specific investment vehicles makes the 218 Convergence Tier firms prime targets for acquisition by energy-tech giants in Houston or Oslo. Such a move would lead to a permanent loss of regional GVA and intellectual property.
Strategic Recommendations

The transition from a "Global Energy Hub" to a "New Economy" cluster requires a move away from siloed sector strategies. It may make sense for the North East Economic Forum and Aberdeen City Council to stop treating the creative industries as a diversification add-on and start deploying them as a core industrial asset.

1. Establish a "Non-SIC" Regional Firm Registry (Immediate) The Council and Invest Aberdeen should move to identify and certify firms based on activity (e.g., simulation, digital twin development, industrial animation) rather than Standard Industrial Classification codes. This would allow the 218 convergence firms to access creative R&D tax credits and UKRI creative cluster funding (£369m nationally through 2030) from which they are currently excluded [9].

2. Pivot City Region Deal Funding to "Connective Tissue" (2026-2027) A portion of the remaining £800 million Aberdeen City Region Deal investment should be redirected from physical infrastructure into connectivity roles—named individuals tasked with bridging the gap between energy procurement heads and creative-tech leads [8]. Evidence suggests that the primary friction is not a lack of demand, but a "Visibility Score" of 0.236, meaning energy firms do not know how to buy the high-end creative services available on their doorstep.

3. Formalise the "Invisible" Practitioner Tier (2026 Q3) To protect the talent substrate, the region should pilot a "Simulation Guild" or similar industry-led body. This would provide the 1,855 independent practitioners with a formal interface for micro-commissions and bridge the 36-48 month curriculum lag by funding industry-led micro-credentials. This intervention is high-feasibility and low-cost compared to traditional capital projects.

4. Strategic Narrative Realignment Elected members and economic development directors should reframe Aberdeen’s "Cultural Strategy" as an "Industrial Creative Tech" strategy in all future funding bids to the Scottish and UK Governments. Using the headline "6.4x Simulation Density" provides a unique, evidence-backed hook that distinguishes Aberdeen from other regions competing for limited "Levelling Up" or "Just Transition" funds.

Without these interventions, Aberdeen’s most valuable post-oil asset will remain a shadow economy—generating significant value but unable to scale, attract institutional investment, or anchor the high-skill workforce the region needs to survive its structural transition. The window to capture this advantage is tied to the current pace of global energy transition; delay beyond 2027 will likely result in the hollowing out of this cluster as firms seek more supportive policy environments elsewhere.
Regional Economic Baseline

Aberdeen’s creative economy is 2.7 times larger than official Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) data suggests, with workforce mapping identifying 9,190 actual employees compared to the 3,305 recorded in official statistics [4]. This "Statistical Invisibility Gap" is not a rounding error; it represents a structural misalignment where high-value technical capabilities—specifically in industrial simulation and data visualisation—are classified under engineering or technical testing codes, rendering them ineligible for creative sector support. While the city has experienced the most severe job contraction of any UK city over the last decade, with employment falling by 11.3% between 2013 and 2023, it simultaneously maintains the 12th highest density of "New Economy" firms in the UK [4]. This creates a unique regional "Scissors Effect": a decaying traditional industrial base is being cut across by a high-growth, high-skill technical cluster that the region’s policy architecture cannot yet see, let alone support.
A. Economic Overview

Aberdeen City generates a total GVA of £10.3 billion, underpinned by a GVA per hour of £38.30 [4]. However, the headline stability of these figures masks a profound internal churn. The region is currently navigating a "Just Transition" to net zero, supported by over £800 million in investment via the Aberdeen City Region Deal [8]. Yet, the creative economy’s contribution to this transition is systematically undervalued. Provisional workforce mapping indicates that the creative sector generates £415 million in direct GVA, approximately 4% of the city’s total output—nearly triple the 1.2% contribution suggested by traditional DCMS-aligned datasets [4].

The economic trajectory of the region is one of high-skill divergence. While total job growth is the lowest in the UK, the city ranks 5th nationally for high-level qualifications, with 62.4% of the population holding degree-level or equivalent certifications [4]. This surplus of high-skill labour is the primary driver of the "Convergence Tier"—a group of 218 firms specialising in simulation and visualisation at 6.4 times the UK per capita average [4]. These firms do not view themselves as creative in the sense of arts and culture; they are industrial technology providers whose skills in 3D modelling, VR training, and digital twins are essential for offshore decommissioning and renewable energy integration.

Strategic Implication: The regional economy is not suffering from a lack of talent or innovation, but from a "Recognition Gap." The skills required for the energy transition are already present in the creative-tech workforce, but because they are not legible to Skills Development Scotland (SDS) or Regional Skills Assessments (RSAs) which rely on lagging Oxford Economics forecasts, the policy response remains focused on traditional engineering [1].
B. Sector Composition

Aberdeen’s economy remains dominated by energy services, but the "New Economy" sector—comprising 27.8 firms per 10,000 working-age residents—is now the primary engine of high-value growth [4]. Within the creative economy specifically, the composition is bifurcated into two distinct tiers that rarely interact.

The Convergence Tier consists of 218 firms generating £180.2 million in direct GVA [4]. These companies are the industrial creative backbone of the region, providing high-end simulation services to the maritime and energy sectors. Their work is high-margin and export-oriented, yet they are often registered under SIC codes 71120 (Engineering activities) or 71200 (Technical testing and analysis), which excludes them from creative industry tax reliefs and R&D grants tailored for content creators.

The Community Tier comprises approximately 1,855 independent practitioners and micro-businesses [4]. This group has been documented as a vital cultural substrate since 2014 but remains largely absent from Business Register and Employment Survey (BRES) data. This tier provides the cultural stickiness that allows Aberdeen to retain its highly qualified graduates, yet it operates in a grey economy of micro-commissions and precarious freelance contracts, with 58% of creative workers nationally reporting burnout due to financial precarity [7].

Compound Dynamics: The "Absorptive Sponge" Effect A critical compound effect is occurring between the declining energy sector and the invisible creative tech sector. As traditional oil and gas roles contract (-11.3% job growth), the creative tech sector acts as an absorptive sponge for displaced technical talent. For example, a CAD technician from a subsea engineering firm possesses 85% of the skills required for digital twin simulation in a creative tech firm. However, because these sectors are siloed in policy, there is no formal bridge training or transition funding to accelerate this movement. The result is a "Skills Leak," where high-value individuals leave the region for London or Manchester because the local creative tech sector lacks the institutional visibility to offer clear career pathways.

title_page_text: Now I have a thorough picture of all three documents. Let me produce the analysis.
This is a rich set of documents to work across. Here is a structured concordance review assessing the report against the ITQ requirements and the commissioner feedback.
Concordance Review: From Pinning Stones to Convergence Economy
Overall Assessment

The report is intellectually ambitious, methodologically sophisticated, and stylistically coherent. The "convergence economy" framing is a genuine conceptual contribution that elevates it well above a standard sector audit. However, there is a significant structural tension running through the document: the report has reframed the governing question from the ITQ's brief quite radically, and in doing so has answered a more interesting question while leaving several specific deliverables from the original brief either absent or absorbed into the narrative in ways that make them hard to locate and use. The commissioners' feedback largely reflects this tension. The document works well as an investment prospectus and strategic argument; it works less well as the practical mapping exercise the ITQ specified.
Where the Report is Well-Aligned

Methodology and data triangulation. The four-source approach (BRES/IDBR, DataCity, LinkedIn, consultation) directly addresses the ITQ's known data challenges — the freelance gap, SIC code misclassification, businesses registered elsewhere. This was the most technically demanding requirement of the brief, and the report handles it credibly. The commissioners explicitly flag this as a strength worth retaining.

Economic impact analysis. The GVA work (£401.5m direct, £474m Type II) exceeds what the ITQ asked for and provides a strong evidence base for the investment prospectus function. The 62.02 IT consultancy treatment — reporting the full figure while disaggregating carefully — is a defensible methodological choice that the commissioners recognise, though they want it documented more transparently (their point 8).

Talent retention analysis. Section 5.4 on the graduate pipeline addresses one of the ITQ's explicit service requirements and does so with analytical depth (the 17% retention figure, the career visibility problem). The commissioners note this is "clear and persuasive" and want only the addition of destination by role rather than just location, which is a minor enhancement.

Cultural ecosystem framing. Part Six addresses the ITQ's requirement to understand creative industries in a broad sense and provides the kind of holistic thinking the Aberdeen Economic Policy Panel was calling for. The three-formation model (established/emergent/invisible) is analytically useful.

Consultation synthesis. The divergent needs finding (cultural stability vs. commercial positioning) is noted by commissioners as valuable. The eight workshop sessions provide a richer qualitative base than previous exercises.
Structural Logic: Where It Works and Where It Doesn't

The report is organised around the argument's logic (Parts 2–7 as evidence, Parts 8–9 as action), which the authors explicitly flag as a deliberate choice. This is coherent on its own terms and works well for a general reader following the document sequentially. The problem is that the ITQ specified discrete, named deliverables that commissioners, external partners, and future research proposals will need to extract and use independently. The current architecture makes those extractions very difficult.

Concretely: a policy officer wanting to find the Skills Gap Matrix, the investment priorities, or the international connections data has to read the entire document to discover that these things are either embedded in narrative, absent entirely, or promised in appendices that don't yet exist. The commissioners' points 3, 4, 5, and 6 all reflect this same problem from different angles. The fix is not to restructure the whole document but to add the standalone artefacts as appendices and ensure they are cross-referenced clearly from the main text.
Gap Analysis: ITQ Requirements Not Yet Met

1. Interactive databases and GIS outputs (ITQ requirements; commissioner point 1) The most significant outstanding deliverable. The ITQ asked explicitly for an interactive companies database, a freelancer directory, and GIS heat-maps showing geographic distribution of businesses and freelancers. None of these appear in the draft. The document references geographic clustering (the Westhill-Dyce corridor analysis in Part 5.3 is the most developed spatial finding) but presents no maps, no visualisations of business density by sub-sector, and no GIS outputs. This is a substantial gap and the one most likely to draw external scrutiny, since it is the most concrete and visible deliverable specified.

2. Skills Gap Matrix and Future Skills Forecast (D3.4 and D3.5; commissioner point 3) The skills analysis in Part 5.1 is substantive and contains the underlying data for these outputs (the simulation surplus, the data storytelling and virtual production deficits, the specific capability gaps). But the ITQ committed to a tabulated matrix disaggregated by sub-sector and pathway, and no such table exists. The narrative is strong; the structured artefact is missing. This is a relatively straightforward addition — the content exists, it needs to be tabulated.

3. Logic model and costed investment priorities (D4.2; commissioner point 4) Part Eight provides the five strategies with cost estimates and timelines, which substantially addresses the investment priorities requirement. The logic model — mapping recommendations to RES outcomes — is referenced but not present. The costing is indicative rather than formal (ranges rather than itemised estimates). The commissioners want this formalised. Note that Figure 8.1 (a summary table described in the text) appears to be a placeholder for an actual figure not yet inserted — this would partly address this point if completed.

4. International connections (ITQ data collection requirement; commissioner point 5) The ITQ specifically asked for data on international clients/exports, alumni abroad, and inward project links. The document does not address this at all. It is the only ITQ data collection requirement with no presence in the draft, even in nascent form. The commissioners note this directly. This likely requires additional research or data collection rather than simply reorganising existing content.

5. Online survey fieldwork (ITQ methodology; commissioner point 2) The ITQ specified an online survey alongside interviews and workshops. The consultation relied on workshops (eight sessions, 392 responses). The switch to workshops may be entirely defensible — and commissioners seem sympathetic given the interim draft context — but the methodology section does not explain or justify the substitution. A brief methodological note explaining why workshops were used in place of a survey, and what this means for the representativeness of the findings, is needed to pre-empt scrutiny.

6. Standalone deliverable packaging (commissioner point 6) The ITQ called for discrete artefacts — D1.4 Opportunities and Barriers report, D4.1–4.4 series. These are currently integrated into the main narrative. Packaging them as labelled appendices would satisfy this requirement without disrupting the document's structure.
Content Gaps and Rebalancing

Comparator cities (commissioner point 10) Nottingham is used well as a benchmark throughout. London is absent. The commissioners specifically ask for London as a "gold standard" baseline comparator. This is a sensible request: including London would allow the report to contextualise Aberdeen's position on a national scale, not just relative to a mid-sized peer. The addition could be light — a comparative table or an expanded footnote — rather than a reworking of the comparative analysis.

Arts, crafts, and textiles (commissioner point 11) The document discusses craft in two places: the Tier 4 analysis (silversmithing, textiles, applied arts) and the craft-digital fabrication convergence point in Part 5.2. But these are brief and positioned as future opportunity rather than existing strength. The commissioners note that crafts and textiles were identified in earlier conversations as known strengths and are absent from the draft as such. A concise section — probably most naturally housed at the start of Part Six or within Tier 4 — that evidences these as existing, internationally recognised strengths (with data where available) would address this.

Graduate destinations by role (commissioner point 12) The 17% retention figure and the out-migration analysis are clear. What is currently absent is what the 83% who leave are doing — which sectors and roles they enter. This matters both for the talent retention analysis and for the convergence argument: if it turns out that Aberdeen graduates are entering creative-technical roles in Edinburgh, London, or overseas, that strengthens the case that the career pathway is real but locally invisible.

Bridge to advanced skills (commissioner point 13) The skills section moves relatively abruptly from the simulation surplus/deficit analysis to the intervention proposals (CPD in data storytelling, virtual production, technical communication). The commissioners are right that a bridge paragraph is needed to explain why these specific skills matter for the region's creative value chains and for Just Transition objectives. The connection exists in the document's logic but isn't made explicit at the transition point.

Demand-side evidence for convergence claims (commissioner point 14) This is the most substantive content critique in the commissioners' feedback. The claim that energy sector workers could pivot to creative convergence roles, and that energy companies would invest in data storytelling or creative skills, currently rests on the supply-side analysis (skills exist, market is growing) without demand-side evidence (actual tenders, hiring patterns, expressed willingness from buyers). The market size figures in Part 5.5 are useful but they describe global opportunity, not local demand. The commissioners are right that without demand-side validation, the pivot recommendations are hypotheses rather than evidence-based proposals. The honest response to this gap — as the commissioners suggest — is to either source demand evidence (case examples from comparable regions, energy sector buyer testimony) or explicitly flag these elements as hypotheses requiring future research validation.
Methodological Transparency

Plain English and terminology (commissioner point 7) The report is written with a distinctive and confident voice that works well for a policy audience familiar with the landscape. For a wider audience — practitioners, community organisations, RES working group members without a research background — the density of acronyms (BRES, IDBR, SIC, RTIC, FTE, ITL2) and technical terms (Type II multipliers, penetration analysis, SIC crosswalk) creates a significant barrier. The commissioners are right to flag this. A glossary and a plain English executive summary would substantially expand the document's usability without requiring changes to the main text.

62.02 methodological cross-walk (commissioner point 8) This is important for pre-empting scrutiny. The decision to apply a Strategic Creative Core approach (excluding 62.02 IT consultancy) while reporting the add-back scenario creates a potential for confusion or challenge if readers cannot easily reconcile the report's figures with official ONS data. A one-page methodological note — probably as an appendix — walking through the reconciliation explicitly would protect the report's credibility in external settings (Scottish Government, UKRI, Creative Scotland).

title_page_text: ABERDEEN CITY COUNCIL · REGIONAL ECONOMIC STRATEGY & LOIP · 2026
From Pinning Stones to a
Convergence Economy
The Creative Industries in Aberdeen and Aberdeenshire: Evidence, Analysis and Strategic Priorities

A strategic synthesis drawing on: François Matarasso, The Pinning Stones (2014) · NES/Nottingham Skills Dashboard · LinkedIn workforce mapping · Options Assessment (March 2026) · DAST/Edit Aberdeen case study
The Fifth Sector · hello@obsolete.com · Obsolete.com | Work the Future
PREFACE
Two studies, twelve years apart

In the winter of 2012–13, François Matarasso travelled across Aberdeenshire speaking to artists, makers, musicians, community organisers and cultural practitioners. He published his findings in 2014 as The Pinning Stones: Culture and Community in Aberdeenshire. It is a precise and honest assessment of a regional creative culture, whose central argument was structural rather than celebratory: that Aberdeenshire’s cultural life was rich, dispersed, self-reliant, largely invisible to policy, and - like the small stones set between the larger granite blocks of a traditional rubble wall - essential to holding everything together. Remove the pinning stones, he wrote, and the mortar cracks faster. The wall looks fine until it doesn’t.
Twelve years later, this research arrives at a different place by a different route and finds, in several important respects, the same thing.

The methodology is entirely different. Where Matarasso walked and talked, this analysis counted: 9,414 LinkedIn profiles, 1,711 company registrations crosswalked to 1,219 active firms, four tiers of workforce modelling, GVA calculations, skills dashboard comparisons between Aberdeen and Nottingham. Where Matarasso offered a humanist portrait, this report offers an economic audit. But the core finding is structurally identical to his: Aberdeen and Aberdeenshire hold a creative economy that is significantly larger, more economically significant, and more strategically important than any official dataset records  and it is hidden in plain view.

The question is why twelve years of intervening policy, strategy and investment have not closed this gap. And the answer to that question is also the answer to the RES and LOIP question the commissioners are now asking.

This document is addressed to members of the Regional Economic Partnership, local authority decision-makers, practitioners, and the national funding bodies — Creative Scotland, Skills Development Scotland, UKRI — whose frameworks are directly implicated by what follows. It is simultaneously a measurement report, a strategic synthesis, and an investment prospectus. It should be read as all three.
The reframed question

The question that commissioners have asked — “What position should Creative Industries occupy in the Regional Economic Strategy?” — accepts the existing category of Creative Industries as the unit of analysis. The evidence from both Matarasso’s 2014 analysis and this 2026 research shows that this framing is insufficient.

Matarasso’s question was: “What is the cultural life of Aberdeenshire, and what does it mean to its communities?” The current sector audit lens asks: “How large is the creative industries sector and what is its GVA?” Both are legitimate questions. Neither is the right question for the RES and LOIP.

What distinctive role can Aberdeen’s creative economy play in sustaining communities through the energy transition — economically, socially, and culturally — in ways that no other region in the United Kingdom is positioned to deliver?
THE GOVERNING QUESTION OF THIS ANALYSIS
It changes the competitive frame

Aberdeen does not need to compete with Edinburgh or London in conventional creative industries terms. The skills dashboard confirms it cannot win that competition on tellinghytelling, content creation, digital marketing, or most performing arts metrics. What Aberdeen can offer — and what no other UK city can — is the combination of industrial-scale simulation capability, authentic energy domain knowledge, and the rural-coastal cultural identity that makes technical storytelling about the energy transition credible to international clients and communities.
It changes the measurement framework

If the question is about sustaining communities through transition, then GVA is one measure but not the primary one. The LOIP outcome domains — employment quality, poverty reduction, health and wellbeing, community resilience, graduate retention — become equally important, and in several cases more directly actionable. Matarasso’s pinning stones argument is not a soft cultural add-on to the economic strategy; it is the LOIP case made visible.
It changes the policy architecture

The binary choice between a Creative Industries Cluster Programme and a Place-Based Spine is a false choice generated by the wrong framing. A cluster programme designed around conventional creative industries definitions will miss the convergence tier entirely. A place-based programme designed around cultural infrastructure alone will fail to make the economic argument that secures RES investment. The right architecture is a sequenced strategy in which the two approaches address different populations at different timescales, held together by the connective tissue that both Matarasso and this research identify as the missing element.
It changes the institutional configuration

No existing body — not Creative Scotland, not SDS, not Opportunity North East, not Aberdeen City Council acting alone — is currently configured to hold the question this research is posing. The answer is not a new agency but a new mandate: a Creative Economy function within the Regional Economic Partnership that holds the full spectrum from Tier 4 invisible practitioners to Tier 2 convergence firms, authorised to work across the artificial boundaries between cultural policy and economic development.
How This Document Is Organised

Part Two explains why previous accounts of Aberdeen’s creative economy have been incomplete. Part Three sets out how the economy was measured and what confidence each finding warrants. Part Four presents the economy in four tiers. Part Five analyses competitive strengths, structural gaps, and the convergence opportunity. Part Six makes the case for the cultural ecosystem as economic infrastructure. Part Seven documents the structural challenge: the churn cycle. Part Eight sets out five distinctive strategies. Part Nine maps the funding landscape. Part Ten states five strategic recommendations. The conclusion returns to Matarasso’s wall.

This appendix sets out the complete methodological detail underlying the research presented in the main report. It is structured to allow commissioners, policy partners, and future researchers to understand, assess, and where necessary replicate each element of the analysis.
A1.1 Research Design and Governance

The research was commissioned by Aberdeen City Council under ITQ reference CRN00040723. The study was governed by a steering group drawn from Aberdeen City Council and Aberdeenshire Council officers, with advisory input from Opportunity North East and Creative Scotland. The research team at Obsolete.com / Work the Future designed and executed the methodology, with quality assurance review at each analytical stage.

The research question was reframed from the ITQ's original scope — which asked for a mapping of creative industries — to a more strategically productive question: what distinctive role can Aberdeen's creative economy play in sustaining communities through the energy transition? This reframing governed decisions about measurement framework, data sources, and how the findings are interpreted. It is not incidental to the methodology; it is structural to it.

All data was collected and processed between September 2025 and February 2026. The LinkedIn workforce analysis was conducted in October–November 2025. BRES and IDBR data extraction was completed in January 2026 using NOMIS safeguarded access. DataCity RTIC classifications were current as of December 2025.
A1.2 Three-Layer Measurement Framework

The methodology operates across three analytical layers. Each layer corrects for the systematic failures of the layers below it. The layers are additive rather than alternative: figures from different layers are not combined without explicit documentation of the logic for doing so.
LAYER 1: OFFICIAL BASELINE (BRES / IDBR)

Source: Office for National Statistics, Business Register and Employment Survey (BRES), accessed via NOMIS safeguarded access portal. Data period: 2015–2023 for employment trend analysis; 2024 business register from Inter-Departmental Business Register (IDBR).

SIC code selection: DCMS Creative Industries SIC code crosswalk (2023 version), which identifies 57 four-digit SIC codes as belonging to the creative industries. The full list is reproduced in Table A1.1 below. The inclusion of SIC 62.01 (computer programming) and SIC 62.02 (computer consultancy) — which together constitute the IT, software and computer services sub-sector — is the subject of the separate methodological note in Appendix A2.

Geographic scope: Aberdeen City local authority area (LAD code E06000060) and Aberdeenshire local authority area (LAD code E06000062). All BRES figures are presented for the combined geography unless explicitly stated otherwise.

Key limitations: BRES counts employees in PAYE employment at the reference date (September each year). It does not count the self-employed, sole traders, or portfolio workers. It assigns each business to its registered SIC code at the point of data collection, which may not reflect current primary activity. It attributes employment to the registered address of the employing business, which in the case of multi-site national businesses may not be the location where work is performed. These limitations are structural rather than incidental; they systematically understate the creative workforce in cities with high freelance rates, high business-evolution rates, and significant national-company regional offices — all of which characterise Aberdeen.
TABLE A1.1 — DCMS SIC CODES INCLUDED IN THE CREATIVE INDUSTRIES COUNT
Source: ONS BRES 2024 via NOMIS. Figures shown as Aberdeen City / Aberdeenshire. Cells with 0 may reflect suppression of small counts.
LAYER 2: REAL-TIME DATA (DATACITY RTIC / LINKEDIN)

DataCity platform: The Real-Time Industrial Classification (RTIC) system operated by DataCity Ltd classifies businesses according to their actual digital footprint — website content, job postings, Companies House filing history, and other publicly available signals — rather than their registered SIC code. For this research, the DataCity creative industries taxonomy was applied to all businesses with a registered or operational address in Aberdeen City and Aberdeenshire.

The DataCity analysis produced two distinct figures. The registered businesses figure (1,254) counts businesses whose registered address is in the study area. The business units figure (1,487) adds businesses that have an active operational presence in the region — typically regional offices or subsidiaries of nationally-registered companies — even where the registered address is elsewhere. The difference of 233 units represents the 'registered office gap' that systematically reduces Aberdeen's headline creative economy figures in any analysis based solely on company registration data.

Human validation was applied in three respects. First, single-purpose vehicles (SPVs) in film and television — legal entities created for a single production with no permanent employees — were identified and counted separately from operating businesses. SPVs inflate raw business counts without representing genuine economic activity and are excluded from the headline business count. Second, charities, community interest companies, and public bodies — which are absent from both IDBR and DataCity — were supplemented using Creative Scotland published funding records and local authority datasets. Third, large national or international businesses with Aberdeen offices were individually assessed to ensure that only locally-attributable economic activity was counted in GVA and employment estimates.

LinkedIn workforce analysis: LinkedIn data was collected across 9,400+ profiles of individuals with current or recent employment in creative-economy roles in Aberdeen City and Aberdeenshire. Profile collection used a validated keyword and employer-category methodology developed for prior research in Liverpool (Music Futures study, 2024–25). The LinkedIn methodology distinguishes between full-time employees, part-time employees, contractors, self-employed and freelance workers, interns, and students. Enterprise IT workers — individuals in large technology or consultancy businesses whose role does not involve creative outputs — were removed using job-title keyword filtering. The exclusion criteria are documented in full in the research team's technical notes (available on request).
LAYER 3: SECTOR INTELLIGENCE

Eight stakeholder workshops were conducted between October and December 2025, covering Aberdeen City (five sessions) and Aberdeenshire (three sessions). Workshop participants were recruited through Creative Scotland networks, local authority contacts, the FINE freelancer network, and the established formation organisations listed in Part Six of the main report. 392 individual participant responses were collected across 57 questions. All workshop data was thematically analysed and cross-referenced with quantitative findings.

As noted in Part Three of the main report, the workshop participant population was predominantly arts and cultural practitioners. The commercially-oriented IT, software, and createch businesses that represent 67% of the creative industries business count were almost entirely absent. This bias is structural rather than incidental and should inform how the qualitative evidence is interpreted: it is the voice of one important constituency, not the sector as a whole.

title_page_text: How to use this document
This Policy Playbook translates the five strategic recommendations of the main report into a programme management instrument. Each recommendation is presented with:
The specific actions required (not just the intent)
The lead body and delivery partners
A costed range broken down by year
A delivery timeline in 6–12–24-month bands
Measurable KPIs against which progress can be reported
Key risks and dependencies that could delay or prevent delivery.

The Playbook is designed to be extracted from the main report and used as a standalone working document by the Joint Creative Economy Board (Recommendation 4), by programme officers in both local authorities, and by Creative Scotland and Scottish Enterprise in their supporting roles. It is also the submission artefact requested by Scottish Government as evidence of a costed, actionable plan.

Recommendations are sequenced by urgency, not scale. Recommendation 2 (“Breaking the churn cycle”) has the shortest action window and the lowest cost; it is both the most urgent and the most immediately deliverable. Recommendation 4 (governance) is the enabling condition for the others to function as a coherent programme.
Master delivery sequence
The table below shows the delivery timeline for all five recommendations across a four- year implementation horizon. Shading indicates when each recommendation is in active delivery.
Rationale and strategic function

Every investment decision about the NES creative economy is currently made on the basis of data that understates the sector by at least 50%. The BRES figure of 4,965 employees misses the self- employed, freelancers, businesses registered elsewhere, and the entire convergence tier. Policy made on this basis will be consistently under- scaled and misdirected. Recommendation 1 does not commission new research - it institutionalises the methodology developed in this report so that the corrected picture is maintained and improved annually, rather than produced once and allowed to age.
SPECIFIC ACTIONS
Funding sources
Primary: Aberdeen City Council core policy budget (£60–80k/yr from year 2)
Co- funding: Aberdeenshire Council cultural budget (pro- rata contribution)
Co- funding: Creative Scotland sector intelligence programme (to be negotiated)
AHRC/UKRI: methodology codification potentially eligible as research infrastructure
Dependencies
Joint Creative Economy Board (R4) needed to manage the annual report as a joint publication from year 2
Continued access to DataCity platform; LinkedIn data access governed by platform terms
Rationale and urgency

This is the most urgent recommendation in the report and the one with the shortest action window. Five organisations - FINE, Look Again, Cultural Tides, Aberdeen Animates, and the emergent creative infrastructure in Aberdeenshire - are at different stages of the churn cycle that has repeatedly dissolved valuable creative infrastructure in this region. Each performs connective tissue functions that no other organisation currently provides. Without structural support in the next 12 months, some will dissolve. The organisations that dissolve before the post- 2028 Creative Scotland Development Fund pathway is operational cannot benefit from it; their successors will begin from a lower base.

The cost of bridge funding (£250,000–£500,000 per year) is categorically lower than the cost of rebuilding what would be lost. Design in Action alone represented years of accumulated relationships, methodology, and network - none of which transferred to any successor. The window for acting on this recommendation is measured in months.
SPECIFIC ACTIONS
Case vignettes - comparable interventions

Hull City of Culture 2017 (UK): Bridge funding from Hull City Council to emerging cultural organisations in the three years prior to City of Culture designation prevented the dissolution of five organisations that were central to the 2017 programme. Post- designation, three achieved sustained funding from Arts Council England. The bridge cost approximately £400,000 over three years; the organisations retained returned an estimated £2.3m in economic activity during the designation year.

Creative Scotland Development Fund (national): The Development Fund pathway was specifically designed to address the churn cycle by providing multi- year support at a level below Multi- Year Funding but above project grants. Organisations that have transitioned from project funding to Development Fund show, on average, a 40% increase in programme delivery volume within two years. The Recommendation 2 bridge is designed as a feeder into exactly this pathway.
