title_page_text: Good to know — the document I've extracted is the full combined playbook and RES recommendations. Let me analyse it now and give you my suggested changes.Here are my suggested changes, working through the document section by section.
Document-level

There's a date inconsistency: the cover says "April 2026" but the footer reads "March 2026." The footer should be updated. The dual attribution (The Fifth Sector on the cover; Obsolete.com / Work the Future in the footer and in R1 and R5 action tables) is also unexplained to any reader who hasn't seen the main report — a brief parenthetical note clarifying that Obsolete.com / Work the Future are the research delivery partners would help, especially since this document is intended as a standalone submission to Scottish Government.
Recommendation 1

The BRES figure of 4,965 employees in the rationale is consistent with the playbook's own language but the main report at several points uses 3,305. If 4,965 is the correct combined City/Shire figure (which it appears to be), the main report should be corrected — but at minimum the playbook should note explicitly that the figure covers both Aberdeen City and Aberdeenshire, since readers comparing it to national datasets may find a discrepancy.

The methodology codification action lists "Obsolete.com / Work the Future (handover)" as lead, with knowledge transfer incompleteness cited as a key risk. That risk is real but the action doesn't specify when the handover must be complete or what the handover product looks like. Recommend adding a deliverable: a methodology document in a format replicable by ACC policy staff without research team involvement, to be signed off by month 4.
Recommendation 2

The rationale refers to "five organisations" but the action table names only four (FINE, Look Again, Cultural Tides, Aberdeen Animates), with "the emergent creative infrastructure in Aberdeenshire" as an unnamed fifth. Either name that fifth organisation or remove the reference to "five" — leaving it vague weakens the urgency argument and invites questions from funders about which organisation you're not naming and why.

The Cultural Tides action is made conditional on UKSPF successor clarity. That conditional framing is appropriate, but the risk it creates — that one of the five bridge grants simply doesn't get awarded in year 1 — should be elevated to the programme-level risk register, not left embedded in an action table. The risk register currently doesn't mention UKSPF succession at all.

The Gray's/Edit formalisation action shows "No direct cost." It will require at minimum coordination time and possibly a small programme budget for mentoring or placement activity. "Officer time + small programme budget TBC" would be more accurate.
Recommendation 3

The KPI for the first action says "MOU signed by all partners by March 2026." The document is dated April 2026. Either that milestone has been met (in which case say so — it strengthens the playbook) or it hasn't (in which case the date needs updating and the delay should be noted). Leaving an already-elapsed deadline unmarked looks like an oversight to any external reviewer.

NESCol appears in the CPD action tables as a delivery partner but not in the MOU action. If NESCol is expected to co-deliver CPD, they need to be party to the partnership agreement from the start, not brought in later.
Recommendation 4

"NESREP Programme Manager" appears once in the action table (as a partner for the RES creative economy chapter) with no explanation of what NESREP is. Add a footnote: "NESREP: North East Scotland Regional Economic Partnership, the body responsible for overseeing the Regional Economic Strategy." Without it, any reader who isn't already inside the NES governance world won't know who is being asked to do what.

More substantively: the action to "Adopt RES creative economy chapter" is scheduled for Year 2. This is too late. The entire research was commissioned in support of the RES, and the commissioning brief specifically asked what position creative industries should occupy in the Regional Economic Strategy. If the creative economy chapter isn't in the RES until Year 2, the report's central purpose — influencing the strategy — will have been missed. Recommend bringing this forward to Months 6–9, with a draft chapter commissioned at the same time as the Joint Board's terms of reference are agreed. The Joint Creative Economy Officer (if appointed by Month 6) can lead this; it doesn't need to wait for the Board to be fully operational.

There's also no mention of the Local Outcomes Improvement Plan anywhere in the playbook. The main report explicitly frames the research as addressing both the RES and the LOIP question. Both local authorities' LOIP should be a named destination for the creative economy chapter — cultural infrastructure, community resilience, and the graduate retention evidence all map directly to LOIP outcomes. Add a brief action: "Align creative economy chapter to both LAs' LOIP frameworks: identify named LOIP outcomes supported by the creative economy and ensure they appear in both the RES chapter and annual measurement reporting."
Recommendation 5

The Creative Career Bridge pilot is scheduled for Year 2. Given the JTF application (also Year 2) will need to evidence demand for the programme, it would strengthen the application to have at least a pilot design document or employer expressions of interest completed in Year 1 rather than the full cohort launching in Year 2. Recommend splitting the action: pilot design and employer engagement in Months 6–12, cohort launch from Year 2.

The policy alignment action ("one-page mapping of recommendations to Screen Scotland/NETS, Creative Scotland skills/funding levers") is assigned to the Joint Creative Economy Officer, with a Month 6 deadline. But the Joint Creative Economy Officer isn't expected to be in post until Month 6. This action either needs to start earlier under interim ACC lead, or the deadline should move to Month 9.
Risk register

The reference to "R3, R5, S1" in the convergence identity risk is a clear error — "S1" is never defined in the playbook. The main report uses "Strategy" numbering in Parts Eight and Nine; this looks like a reference to Strategy 1 from that section that was carried across without translation. It should either be replaced with the corresponding recommendation number or explained.

Two risks are missing that the evidence supports adding. First, Creative Scotland funding landscape change: CS is named as a co-funder in R1, R2, and R3, but the playbook doesn't acknowledge that CS's own funding position (particularly post-NPO settlement) is uncertain. Second, key personnel dependency: several named organisations (FINE, Look Again) carry single-person dependency risk, and the Joint Creative Economy Officer role — central to programme delivery — will take time to recruit and embed. Both warrant a line in the programme-level register.
Cost summary

The R2 Year 1 figure of £300–500k sits ambiguously against the action table, where the Creative Ecology Structural Fund is described as "£250–500k/yr shared" between the two LAs. It would help to clarify whether the cost summary figures represent total cost (both LAs combined) or net LA contribution after co-funding — currently that distinction isn't explicit, which matters when the document is used as a budget submission.
Offer to implement

If you'd like, I can produce an updated version of the document with these changes applied as tracked changes — that way you can accept or reject each one individually before it goes anywhere. Just say the word.

Post- designation, three achieved sustained funding from Arts Council England. The bridge cost approximately £400,000 over three years; the organisations retained returned an estimated £2.3m in economic activity during the designation year.

Creative Scotland Development Fund (national): The Development Fund pathway was specifically designed to address the churn cycle by providing multi- year support at a level below Multi- Year Funding but above project grants. Organisations that have transitioned from project funding to Development Fund show, on average, a 40% increase in programme delivery volume within two years. The Recommendation 2 bridge is designed as a feeder into exactly this pathway.
Rationale and opportunity

UKRI's CoSTAR (Creative Scale- Up Technology and Research) programme represents the largest available UK investment in creative industries convergence. Aberdeen's typological differentiation - energy- creative convergence in an oil transition economy, with a simulation surplus four times the UK average - is a compelling case for CoSTAR cluster investment that Edinburgh, Glasgow, and London cannot replicate. The Aberdeen–Dundee Creative Technology Corridor combines Aberdeen's simulation surplus with Abertay University's internationally recognised game design and digital arts strength, creating a corridor with the profile to compete for CoSTAR investment at a scale that neither city could achieve individually.

title_page_text: NORTH EAST SCOTLAND CREATIVE INDUSTRIES MAPPING
From Pinning Stones to
Convergence Economy
Creative Industries in Aberdeen and Aberdeenshire: Evidence, Analysis and Strategic Priorities
Commissioned by: Aberdeen City Council  |  Delivered by: The Fifth Sector, Obsolete.com and Unscrambled.world
Two studies, twelve years apart
On continuity, method, and the question that has not yet been answered

In 2014, the cultural researcher François Matarasso completed a study of the arts and creative life of Aberdeen and Aberdeenshire. He called it The Pinning Stones: a term drawn from the drystane dyke tradition of this part of Scotland, in which certain stones are driven through the full width of the wall to bind it together. Remove the pinning stones and the wall collapses. Matarasso's argument was that the region possessed cultural practitioners and organisations who performed exactly this function: they were structurally essential to the coherence of the creative ecosystem, largely invisible to outside observers, and chronically underfunded relative to their importance.

Twelve years later, this research arrives at substantially the same structural conclusion through an entirely different methodology. Where Matarasso worked qualitatively, through observation, conversation, and cultural analysis, this study deploys diverse forms of data and direct consultation with practitioners across both local authority areas to analyse the economic condition of the creative sector and its workforce. The methods are markedly different; the findings reflect the same structural weaknesses reflected in the previous study.

The creative economy of North East Scotland is significantly larger than official accounts suggest but the practitioners who sustain its foundations are systematically invisible to the measurement frameworks that govern public investment. And twelve years of policy have not closed the gap between what this economy is and what institutional support it receives.

This is not a counsel of despair. The twelve-year interval has also produced something that Matarasso could not see in 2014, because it did not yet fully exist: a convergence between Aberdeen's deep engineering and energy expertise and its creative capabilities that represents one of the most distinctive economic development opportunities in the United Kingdom. The energy transition, the shift away from fossil fuel dependence that is simultaneously Aberdeen's greatest structural challenge and its most significant strategic opportunity, is generating demand for exactly the skills this region has been quietly accumulating for decades.

This document is the synthesis of that finding. It is both an evidence base and an argument. It seeks to be read not as a sector audit but as an answer to a question about what kind of economy Aberdeen and Aberdeenshire can build, and for whom.
The pinning stones are still in place. This research has counted them, valued them, and located them on a map. What they now need is not admiration but mortar.
PART ONE
Who should read this report?
1.1 Scope and Purpose

This document is addressed to members of the North East Scotland Creative Industries Working Group, local authority decision-makers in Aberdeen City Council and Aberdeenshire Council, and the national funding bodies (including Creative Scotland, Skills Development Scotland, and UKRI) whose frameworks are directly implicated in its recommendations. It will also be of direct relevance to Opportunity North East and to the Scottish Enterprise teams responsible for regional economic development.
It is simultaneously three things: a measurement report, a strategic synthesis, and an investment prospectus.
As a measurement report, it establishes the true scale and significance of the creative economy of North East Scotland, how it is composed, and where it sits relative to comparable regions.
As a strategic synthesis, it draws on that measurement to identify where the distinctive opportunities lie and what is preventing them from being realised.
As an investment prospectus, it translates both into specific, costed, sequenced recommendations that local and national bodies can act on within existing governance and funding frameworks.

The research was commissioned in support of the development of North East Scotland Regional Economic Strategy and specifically the strategy's commitment to a fair transition to an economy less dependent on oil and gas. That framing is not incidental to this document: it governs both what has been measured and how the findings are interpreted.
1,487  Creative businesses identified - 50% more than ONS data indicated
£401.5m  GVA contribution from the creative economy (ONS regional methodology)
7,500+  Total workforce including estimated 2,050 unmapped freelance workers
1.2 Reframing the governing question

Everything that follows in this document depends on asking the right question. The wrong question has shaped creative industries policy in this region - and in Scotland more broadly - for at least a decade. It has produced strategies that are technically competent and practically limited, because they are answers to the wrong thing.
THE QUESTION THAT HAS GOVERNED POLICY TO DATE
How do we grow the creative industries sector?
THE QUESTION THIS RESEARCH IS DESIGNED TO ANSWER

title_page_text: North East Scotland Creative Industries Research
Draft report
Prepared for Aberdeen City Council and Aberdeenshire Council
by Iain Bennett, Jon Bains and Lynne McCadden of The Fifth Sector and Simon Sprince and Andy Goodwin of unscrambled.world
5 February 2026
1. Economic Scale and Significance of Creative Industries
1.1 Approach and methodology

Accurate measurement of creative industries presents specific challenges due to high levels of freelance labour, micro-enterprises, and rapid digital evolution. Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) codes provide a robust framework for assessing registered company structures and formal employment but capture less detail regarding the agile, project-based workforce common in this sector.
To address this, this report employs a stepwise methodology that triangulates three distinct layers of evidence to build the most likely economic scenario:

Official baseline: Office for National Statistics (ONS) data (safeguarded data accessed via Nomisweb): the Business Register and Employment Survey (BRES) for employment and Inter-Departmental Business Register (IDBR) for companies data.

Real-time data: AI-driven analysis of registered businesses from Data City and employment status data derived from analysis of LinkedIn. This present us with a number of advantages, including real-time data on companies an insights into freelance, self-employed and contract working not recorded in official employment statistics.

Sector intelligence: Qualitative and quantitative validation derived from review of existing academic and industry reports, primary research including industry consultation, and workshops with local stakeholders.
1.2 Official baseline (BRES and IDBR)

The analysis begins with the official ONS data which serves as the foundation for our modelling. The sampling approach used in BRES to estimate creative industries employment provides the "floor" of sector activity.

IDBR data provides evidence of the base of “active” businesses registered to addresses in Aberdeen and Aberdeenshire; as in all parts of the UK, it reveals a high density of micro-businesses. Over 90% of registered creative enterprises in the region employ fewer than 10 people. This fragmentation contributes to a view that official counts significantly underreport the actual creative workforce, as national statistics often miss non-PAYE freelancers and directors of micro-limited companies who are remunerated via dividends rather than salary.
1.3 Defining the Strategic Creative Core

A critical step in this analysis involves refining the definition of the Creative Industries to reflect the specific economic context of Aberdeen City and Shire, and to minimise the risk of “double counting” economic activity and employment – specifically, to avoid duplicating outputs already identified by ONE’s 2023 report into the region’s Digital Tech sector.

Official data indicates substantial employment in IT Consultancy (SIC 62.02) which generates an estimated £150m in GVA. Although formally part of the Creative Industries, detailed sector intelligence and stakeholder consultation suggests this activity acts primarily as enterprise support for the region's wider economy, with clear linkages in particular to the Energy sector, rather than as a generator of creative IP.

To ensure the integrity of the findings, we have therefore excluded general IT consultancy from our measurement and assessment of the Strategic Creative Core. This allows the analysis of digital creative industries to focus on Createch activities (such as software development and publishing, computer games development, VFX, simulation and immersive content production) where both the means of production and the output are explicitly creative.
Following this exclusion, the official employment count for the region's creative sector stands at 3,305 employees.
1.4 Real-Time Evidence (Data City and LinkedIn)
To verify the extent of the creative business base and workforce beyond official counts, we utilised two other proprietary source of date:

Data City’s platform offers a range of tools based on analysis of company website text t and other financial data to distinguish the “real activity of companies, reflected in Real-Time Industrial Classifications (RTICs) which provide a more granular and up-to-the-minute description of company activity when compared to registered SIC codes. This identified a broader population of 1,520 active firms, more than 50% more than shown in IDBR, particularly in Createch, Video Production, and Digital Agency sectors, This includes a cohort of businesses active in the region but registered elsewhere – in some cases subsidiaries of larger firms, but often just a result of companies using their accountant as a registered office address irrespective of their actual business location.

Further validation came from analysis of LinkedIn. We use LinkedIn essentially as a pre-filled survey with a much larger sample frame than official statistics to derive insights into the scale and activity of the workforce. This identified 9,414 unique profiles of residents of the region with occupations in the creative sector. After removing some 4,000 enterprise IT profiles, the remaining 5,422 unique users provided evidence of a workforce split more or less evenly between those employed by firms and those operating independently. This analysis reveals the extent to which the region’s creative workforce is underestimated, with some 2,370 additional creatives who would not appear in official employment statistics.
1.5 Four-Tier Strategic Model

By reconciling official data with digital evidence and validating findings through stakeholder consultation, we arrived at a Four-Tier Employment Structure. This model offers a comprehensive profile of the Strategic Creative Core which implies a total workforce of 7,530.
Each of the four tiers reveals specific industrial strengths unique to the region:
Tier 1 (Institutional Anchors)

Removing IT consultancy firms and software integrators from our analysis of the creative core reveals that there are no commercial “primes” operating in the region’s creative industries; this tier is instead characterised by large-scale employment in culture and heritage. It reflects the region's significant museum and library assets, alongside major cultural infrastructure such as Aberdeen Performing Arts. The relatively low FTE intensity (0.68) is typical of the sector's reliance on part-time, casual and sessional staff for event delivery.

title_page_text: Appendix A: The Regional Creative Funding Landscape, 2020 to 2031

This appendix provides a detailed account of the funding arrangements that sustain the creative and cultural sector in North East Scotland. It covers the period from 2020, when the economic consequences of the pandemic began to reshape the sector's financial architecture, to 2031, the outer horizon of the current planning cycle. It is organised in four sections: national structural funding through Creative Scotland; local authority investment by Aberdeen City Council and Aberdeenshire Council; UKRI and external funding relevant to the convergence economy; and the post-2028 outlook with identified decision points and funding gaps.

The appendix should be read alongside Recommendation 2 (Creative Ecology Structural Fund), Recommendation 3 (CoSTAR bid), and Recommendation 4 (Joint Board), each of which depends on an accurate picture of the current funding landscape and its forward trajectory.
A.1 Creative Scotland Multi-Year Funding, 2025 to 2028

Creative Scotland's Multi-Year Funding (MYF) portfolio, formerly the Regular Funded Organisation framework, provides the primary source of structural revenue funding for the anchor organisations of the regional creative economy. For the 2025 to 2028 period, the following organisations in North East Scotland hold confirmed MYF awards.

Total confirmed MYF investment in North East Scotland for 2025 to 2028: £4.39 million per year across six organisations. This represents a substantial increase on the preceding award period, with uplifts of 34% in Year 1 and 54% from Year 2 onwards across the portfolio, reflecting Creative Scotland's recognition of the funding gap that had accumulated under standstill awards.

The following established organisations in the region are not currently in the MYF portfolio but have a relationship with Creative Scotland through project or programme funding: Scottish Sculpture Workshop (Lumsden), Deveron Projects (Huntly), Haddo Arts, and North East Open Studios. Each has a track record extending back to or before the 2014 Pinning Stones study.
Post-2028 architecture
Creative Scotland has confirmed the following mechanisms for the period after March 2028.

The Development Fund pathway is designed to bring organisations toward full MYF membership from 2026 to 2027 onwards. Thirteen organisations are understood to be in the pipeline nationally. For the North East, Look Again, the Freelance Independents North East network (FINE), and Creative Aberdeenshire Network are the organisations most strategically positioned to access this route, provided they are able to demonstrate financial sustainability and programme track record before the application window opens.

The Creative Scotland core operating support model, targeted for implementation by 2029, represents a further evolution of structural funding toward multi-year revenue relationships rather than project grants. Organisations in the Development Fund pipeline in 2026 to 2027 are the most likely beneficiaries of this model in the North East.

The critical window is 2026 to 2027. Organisations that do not achieve Development Fund status before the post-2028 portfolio review will be competing for a different set of instruments in a more uncertain fiscal environment. The Creative Ecology Structural Fund recommended in Part Ten is designed to bridge the gap between current precarity and Development Fund eligibility.
A.2 Aberdeen City Council: Culture Investment Programme and associated funds
Culture Investment Programme (CIP) and Common Good Fund

Aberdeen City Council's Culture Investment Programme allocates approximately £1.5 million per year across 15 partner organisations through its Common Good Fund in 2025 to 2026. Awards are made through an annual competitive process. The programme supports a range of cultural and creative organisations operating in Aberdeen City, including Look Again. Because funding is allocated annually rather than multi-year, it does not provide the structural security required to break the churn cycle identified in Part Seven.

Named CIP recipients include Aberdeen Performing Arts, Peacock Visual Arts, and a cohort of smaller organisations working in community cultural activity, youth arts, and participation. The full list of 15 partners is available from Aberdeen City Council's Culture team.
Catalyst Fund

The Catalyst Fund is an Aberdeen City Council mechanism designed as a bridge toward Creative Scotland Core Operating Support by 2029. It is intended to support organisations that are developing toward structural funding eligibility but are not yet in a position to apply. It represents the most directly relevant local authority instrument for the emergent formation organisations identified in this report.
Acorn Fund

The Acorn Fund supports micro-commissions and early-stage creative activity in Aberdeen City. It operates at a smaller scale than the CIP and Catalyst Fund and is primarily relevant to Tier 3 and Tier 4 practitioners rather than organisations seeking structural revenue funding.
Pop-up activation infrastructure

Aberdeen City Council's city centre management function has developed a pop-up activation kit: pre-furnished, ready-to-occupy retail spaces designed to reduce the cost and logistical burden for organisations seeking a temporary city centre presence. This initiative, confirmed in April 2026 consultation with Dean McGlynn (Aberdeen City Council City Centre Manager), is being promoted through Aberdeen Inspired and business gateway channels. It is not currently connected to the creative organisations identified in this report. The recommendation in Part Ten that the council's culture team and city centre management function work together to connect Tier 4 practitioners and organisations to this resource follows directly from this gap.
A.3 Aberdeenshire Council: UKSPF and cultural investment
UK Shared Prosperity Fund: Cultural Tides

Aberdeenshire Council secured £170,126 from the UK Shared Prosperity Fund (UKSPF) to support the Cultural Tides initiative in 2024 to 2025. Cultural Tides provided support for cultural activity across Aberdeenshire, operating across the same territory as the dispersed Tier 4 practitioner population documented in Part Four. This represents an important but time-limited investment: UKSPF is a programme with a defined end point, and no direct successor has been confirmed.
Aberdeenshire Council creative economy investment

Aberdeenshire Council does not currently have a standalone creative industries strategy or dedicated creative economy budget line equivalent to Aberdeen City Council's CIP. Creative economy activity is supported primarily through the Cultural Services function, the Live Life Aberdeenshire leisure and cultural trust, and the planning and economic development functions where they intersect with creative activity. The absence of a dedicated budget line is both a measurement gap and a strategic vulnerability: it means that creative economy investment in Aberdeenshire is distributed across multiple budget heads and is not visible as a coherent programme.
Heritage Lottery Fund and capital investment

The Portsoy development, identified in the NES Culture Connects cluster proposals as one of two Aberdeenshire hub investments in the Place-Based Spine cluster option, is subject to ongoing capital fundraising. A Heritage Lottery Fund application is understood to be in preparation. The Banff development, the second identified hub, is at an earlier stage. Both represent capital pipeline investments that would anchor the place-based creative economy argument in specific locations across Aberdeenshire.

title_page_text: From Pinning Stones to Convergence Economy
Strategic synthesis of the role of Creative Industries in the Regional Economic Strategy and Local Outcomes Improvement Plan for Aberdeen and Aberdeenshire
Preface: Two studies, conducted twelve years apart, reveal structural similarities

In the winter of 2012–13, François Matarasso travelled across Aberdeenshire speaking to artists, makers, musicians, community organisers and cultural practitioners. He published his findings in 2014 as The Pinning Stones: Culture and Community in Aberdeenshire. It is a precise and honest assessment of a regional creative culture. Its central argument was structural rather than celebratory: that Aberdeenshire’s cultural life was rich, dispersed, self-reliant, largely invisible to policy, and, like the small stones set between the larger granite blocks of a traditional rubble wall, essential to holding everything together. Remove the pinning stones, he wrote, and the mortar cracks faster. The wall looks fine until it doesn’t.
Twelve years later, this research arrives at a different place by a different route and finds, in several important respects, the same thing. And something more.

The methodology is entirely different. Where Matarasso walked and talked, this analysis counted: LinkedIn profiles, company registrations, four tiers of workforce modelling, gross value added calculations, skills comparisons and place-based counterfactuals. Where Matarasso offered a humanist portrait, this report offers an economic audit. The core finding about scale and visibility is structurally identical to his: the region holds a creative economy that is significantly larger, more economically significant, and more strategically important than any official dataset records, and it is hidden in plain view.

But this research finds something Matarasso’s lens could not have seen in 2014: a second structural asset, visible only to an entirely different set of lenses. The simulation and visualisation firms of the Westhill-Dyce corridor and the creative, marketing, and content agencies of Aberdeen City centre each hold precisely what the other commercially lacks. The gap between them is ten miles and the absence of any institution with the mandate to broker a connection. The analysis does not locate a deficit to be remedied, but locates a trading relationship waiting to be made.

The question is why twelve years of intervening policy, strategy and investment have not closed the visibility gap that Matarasso first documented. The answer to that question is also the answer to the Regional Economic Strategy and Local Outcomes Improvement Plan question the commissioners are now asking.
Part One: What this document is and who it is for
1.1 Scope and purpose

This document presents the findings of a comprehensive assessment of the creative economy of Aberdeen City and Aberdeenshire. It is addressed at once to Regional Economic Partnership members and local authority decision-makers; to practitioners and organisations working across the creative, cultural and digital sectors; and to any reader with an interest in how North East Scotland positions itself for sustained economic growth during a period of rapid structural transition.

It draws on original analysis combining official government data, real-time company intelligence and workforce profiling with stakeholder consultation and comparative research. It makes the case for strategic investment grounded in evidence, identifies specific funding opportunities that are available now, and charts the growth pathways available at each level of a creative economy that is larger, more productive and more strategically distinctive than any previous account has recognised.
1.2 The central finding
The region contains three geographically disparate and commercially disconnected communities:

The creative, marketing, and content production agencies in the City of Aberdeen hold the narrative capability, client management experience, and commissioning relationships through which major contracts flow.

The second community is the one identified by Matarasso’s 2014 study, The Pinning Stones: Culture and Community in Aberdeenshire: distributed and often disconnected creative practitioners from Banff to Fraserburgh to Montrose and across rural Aberdeenshire,

The third group, a cluster of  digital-technical firms collocated alongside the energy and technical services providers in Westhill,  hold world-class technical capability at concentrations far above those of comparable UK cities but have no connection, awareness of or stimulus to connect with the other two groups.

Each is arriving at the limit of what its standalone capability can deliver. Neither currently has a commercial relationship with the other. The separation between them is entirely institutional: a product of geography, sectoral self-identification, and the absence of any mechanism through which a cultural and commercial exchange could be brokered.

This finding sits alongside, and reinforces, the broader finding about scale. The creative economy of North East Scotland accounts for more than 7,500 workers, generates direct gross value added of £315 million, and produces a total annual economic impact of £474 million. Simply acknowledging that there could be greater convergence between those three disparate groups would raise those figures to 8,825 workers, £466 million in GVA and £713 million in total economic impact. These figures are not visible in any current policy framework because the measurement tools applied to date were not designed to find them.
1.3 Reframing the strategic question

The tender for this research asked for evidence to demonstrate the position that creative industries should occupy in Regional Economic Strategy. That framing accepts the existing category of creative industries as the unit of analysis. The evidence from both Matarasso’s 2014 analysis and this 2026 research shows that framing is insufficient.

The question the evidence demands is this: what distinctive role can the creative economy of North East Scotland play in sustaining communities through the energy transition, economically, socially, and culturally, in ways that no other region in the United Kingdom is positioned to deliver?
This reframing has four immediate consequences.

It changes the competitive frame: the region does not need to compete with the Central Belt or London in conventional creative industries terms. What the region can offer, and what no other UK city or region can match, is the combination of industrial-scale simulation capability, authentic energy domain knowledge, and the rural-coastal cultural identity that makes technical storytelling about the energy transition credible to international clients and communities.

It changes the measurement framework: if the question is about sustaining communities through transition, then gross value added is one measure but the Local Outcomes Improvement Plan outcome domains become equally important.

It changes the policy architecture: it removes a false binary choice between investment in digital sectors and creative industries, and argues that the right approach is a sequenced strategy that addresses different populations at different timescales.

It calls for a change to current institutional configuration: no existing body is currently configured to provide solutions that respond to the evidence presented in this research, and the answer is a new mandate rather than a new agency.
1.4 How this document is organised

Part Two documents how the economy was measured across three layers of evidence explains why previous accounts of this economy have understated it, and describes the methodology applied here. Part Three presents a new four-tier economic model and its aggregate findings. Part Four analyses the convergence opportunity, characterising both communities and the market a combined CreaTech offer could address. Part Five correlates data analysis with findings from primary research. Part Six describes the cultural ecosystem as economic infrastructure. Part Six documents the structural challenge of the organisational “churn” that results from time-bound public funding. Part Seven sets out five growth strategies. Part Eight describes the funding landscape and live opportunities. Part Nine provides an options assessment, Part Nine presents five strategic recommendations. Appendices provide the full methodology, skills dashboard data, case studies, funding landscape detail, options assessments and policy playbook.

title_page_text: From Pinning Stones to Convergence Economy
Executive Summary
The starting point

In the winter of 2012–13, François Matarasso spent months travelling across Aberdeenshire, talking to artists, makers, musicians and community practitioners. He published his findings in 2014 as The Pinning Stones: Culture and Community in Aberdeenshire. His central argument was structural rather than celebratory: that the cultural life of the region was rich, dispersed, self-reliant, largely invisible to policy, and, like the small stones set between the larger granite blocks of a traditional rubble wall, essential to holding everything together. Remove the pinning stones, he wrote, and the mortar cracks faster than anyone expects.
This research set out twelve years later by a different route and arrives, in several important respects, at the same place. And at something more.

Where Matarasso walked and talked, this analysis counted: LinkedIn profiles, company registrations, four tiers of workforce modelling, gross value added calculations and skills comparisons. Where he offered a humanist portrait, this report offers an economic audit. The core structural finding is identical to his: the region holds a creative economy significantly larger, more economically significant and more strategically important than any official dataset records, hidden in plain view. The analysis has also found something Matarasso's lens could not have seen in 2014: a second structural asset, visible only through an entirely different set of lenses, in the form of a complementary cluster of creative-technical firms in the Westhill-Dyce corridor, sitting at the intersection of the region's industrial heritage and its creative future.
Why previous accounts have been incomplete

Standard approaches to measuring creative industries rely on two official sources: the Business Register and Employment Survey (BRES), which counts formally employed workers in registered businesses, and the Inter-Departmental Business Register (IDBR), which records companies by their declared Standard Industrial Classification code. Both are authoritative. Both systematically undercount the creative economy in Aberdeen City and Aberdeenshire.

BRES misses the large population of self-employed and freelance practitioners who are neither employed by a firm nor registered as an employer. In a sector where over 90% of enterprises employ fewer than ten people and where many practitioners operate through portfolio working, part-time activity and informal contracts, this is not a marginal omission.

SIC codes record what a company declares itself to be at the point of registration, not what it actually does. A substantial population of firms in the energy, subsea and engineering sectors routinely deploys creative-origin technical skills, including real-time three-dimensional visualisation, simulation, digital twin development and immersive content production, as a core part of its commercial offer. Under standard SIC classification, virtually none appears in creative industries counts.

IT consultancy (SIC 62.02) accounts for between 1,400 and 1,600 jobs and an estimated £150 million in gross value added. Sector intelligence confirms that this activity functions primarily as enterprise support for the energy sector. Including it would inflate the creative economy count while misrepresenting its character. This report excludes it, retaining a methodological crosswalk to allow comparison with national headline figures.
How the creative economy was measured
Three distinct layers of evidence were reconciled through a sequence of analytical steps designed to avoid both double-counting and systematic exclusion.

The first layer is the official baseline. BRES data filtered against creative industries SIC codes and adjusted to remove IT consultancy produces an employment count of approximately 3,300 workers: the floor of the analysis, capturing the region's publicly funded cultural institutions, its registered design and architecture practices, and its commercial creative firms.

The second layer draws on two proprietary real-time sources. The Data City platform analyses company website content to assign Real-Time Industrial Classifications, descriptions of what firms actually do rather than how they are officially classified. LinkedIn analysis, treating the platform as a large pre-filled workforce survey, identified over 8,000 unique profiles of North East residents with creative sector occupations, from which the IT services and consultancy component was excluded, leaving a verified creative workforce of 8,457, adjusted to 8,760 to correct for the known underrepresentation of museums and library workers in LinkedIn data.

The third layer is qualitative and sector-intelligence based: stakeholder workshops, practitioner interviews and comparative studies from other regions, including the Liverpool Music Futures cluster mapping study, whose methodology informed the treatment of shared utility employment in the live music and events economy.

From this triangulation a four-tier model of the strategic creative core was constructed, accounting for a total creative workforce of more than 10,700 people. GVA estimates are derived from ONS regional output data apportioned to SIC codes on the basis of official employment, benchmarked against sector averages from Data City company records and DCMS economic estimates, and adjusted for the full-time equivalent intensity that characterises each tier's employment structure.
The economy in four tiers
Tier 1: Institutional anchors

Comprising 65 publicly funded cultural institutions, museums, libraries and major performing arts venues, Tier 1 accounts for 1,180 workers (800 FTE). Direct GVA is £19 million. A Type II multiplier of 1.40, reflecting stable but restricted public procurement supply chains, produces a total economic impact of £26 million.

The modest direct GVA contribution understates the strategic significance of these organisations. Aberdeen Performing Arts, Peacock Visual Arts, Citymoves Dance Agency, Sound Festival, North East Arts Touring, The Barn and Scottish Sculpture Workshop are economic infrastructure: sustaining audience relationships, graduate placements and professional development pathways that the commercial tiers depend on, and holding the institutional knowledge of a creative ecology whose depth is measured in decades rather than funding cycles. The Creative Scotland Multi-Year Funding portfolio, confirmed for 2025 to 2028 with awards to Aberdeen Performing Arts (£1.69 million), Peacock and The Worm (£1 million), Citymoves Dance Agency (£450,000), Sound Festival (£350,000), North East Arts Touring (£400,000) and The Barn (£500,000), provides the structural security that has distinguished these organisations from those that have not survived the past decade.
Tier 2: SME commercial core

Comprising registered businesses across architecture, design, advertising, creative software, film, television, music, visual and performing arts and related fields, Tier 2 accounts for 4,340 workers (3,950 FTE) and direct GVA of £420 million. A Type II multiplier of 1.60, reflecting extensive local supply chain activity, produces a total economic impact of £672 million. Architecture and the built environment, employing around 400 staff at high full-time intensity, reflects a historical strength sustained by energy legacy and new capital projects in renewables. The creative technology sub-sector, comprising high-value creative software, film, television, video and gaming firms, functions as the region's productivity engine.
Tier 3: Visible freelancers

Comprising 3,240 independent professionals (2,430 FTE) identifying as freelance, self-employed or contractors across advertising, marketing, film, television, video production, games development, photography, publishing and creative technology, Tier 3 generates direct GVA of £115 million. A Type II multiplier of 1.40, driven by local consumption of earnings, produces a total economic impact of £162 million. This tier provides the flexible skilled capacity that allows commercial firms in Tier 2 to scale rapidly for project opportunities without permanent overhead. In a sector characterised by short-term commissions and variable demand, a deep freelance pool is a structural competitive advantage. Only 17% of creative graduates from the region's universities currently remain in North East Scotland after graduating; many of those who do stay enter Tier 3 practice in ways that make them invisible to official counts.
Tier 4: Invisible workforce

Tier 4 cannot be measured directly. It is inferred from penetration gap analysis: the difference between the estimated total population of creative practitioners in low-digital sub-sectors and the proportion identifiable through LinkedIn and official data. The estimate of 1,855 core practitioners (835 FTE) is derived through workspace density modelling, open studio participation records and trade body analysis. A further 180 shared utility workers in hospitality and events are attributed to this tier at a lower intensity, producing a combined total of 2,035 individuals and 860 FTE. Direct GVA is estimated at £28 million; a Type II multiplier of 1.20 produces a total economic impact of £34 million.

Tier 4 is, in Matarasso's terms, where the pinning stones sit. These are the independent artists, makers and musicians who sustain the community infrastructure that makes the region worth living in, carry the craft and making traditions that represent some of its most distinctive cultural strengths, and supply the creative imagination that the commercial tiers draw on. Deemouth Artist Studios in Torry, whose practitioners include internationally trading jewellers with sales through Goldsmiths Fair London and US markets, and the Edit Aberdeen retail model, which generated £100,000 in sales for makers in its most recent year, provide direct evidence of a population generating measurable commercial revenue from a base that BRES records as zero.
Combined four-tier findings

Together the four tiers account for a total creative workforce of more than 10,700 people, generating direct gross value added of £582 million and a total annual economic impact of £894 million. 49% of this workforce works independently as freelancers, sole traders or micro-enterprise operators invisible to standard employment counts. These are not the figures of a peripheral cultural amenity. They are the figures of an economy with the scale to justify serious strategic investment, the distinctiveness to make a credible case for national and international funding, and the structural fragility that makes investment urgent.

title_page_text: How to use this document
This Policy Playbook translates the five strategic recommendations of the main report into a programme management instrument. Each recommendation is presented with:
The specific actions required (not just the intent)
The lead body and delivery partners
A costed range broken down by year
A delivery timeline in 6–12–24-month bands
Measurable KPIs against which progress can be reported
Key risks and dependencies that could delay or prevent delivery.

The Playbook is designed to be extracted from the main report and used as a standalone working document by the Joint Creative Economy Board (Recommendation 4), by programme officers in both local authorities, and by Creative Scotland and Scottish Enterprise in their supporting roles. It is also the submission artefact requested by Scottish Government as evidence of a costed, actionable plan.

Recommendations are sequenced by urgency, not scale. Recommendation 2 (“Breaking the churn cycle”) has the shortest action window and the lowest cost; it is both the most urgent and the most immediately deliverable. Recommendation 4 (governance) is the enabling condition for the others to function as a coherent programme.
Master delivery sequence
The table below shows the delivery timeline for all five recommendations across a four- year implementation horizon. Shading indicates when each recommendation is in active delivery.
Rationale and strategic function

Every investment decision about the NES creative economy is currently made on the basis of data that understates the sector by at least 50%.  Even the higher figure systematically misses the self-employed, freelancers, businesses registered elsewhere, and employees of other software and IT services companies in the “convergence” tier. Policy made on either BRES figure will be under-scaled and misdirected. Recommendation 1 does not commission new research; it institutionalises the methodology developed in this report so that the corrected picture is maintained and improved annually, rather than produced once and allowed to age.
SPECIFIC ACTIONS
Funding sources
Primary: Aberdeen City Council core policy budget (£60–80k/yr from year 2)
Co- funding: Aberdeenshire Council cultural budget (pro-rata contribution)
Co- funding: Creative Scotland sector intelligence programme (to be negotiated)
AHRC/UKRI: methodology codification potentially eligible as research infrastructure
Dependencies
Joint Creative Economy Board (R4) needed to manage the annual report as a joint publication from year 2
Continued access to DataCity platform; LinkedIn data subject to separate contract for analysis
Rationale and urgency

This is the most urgent recommendation in the report and the one with the shortest action window. The organisations that represent different elements of the region’s varied cultural and creative ecology – including FINE, Look Again,  - are at different stages of the churn cycle that has repeatedly dissolved valuable creative infrastructure, and with it the sector intelligence and institutional memory essential to future planning. Each performs connective tissue functions that no other organisation currently provides. Without structural support in the next 12 months, some will dissolve. The organisations that dissolve before the post-2028 Creative Scotland Development Fund pathway is operational cannot benefit from it; their successors will begin from a lower base.

The suggested cost of bridge funding (£250,000–£500,000 per year) is categorically lower than the cost of rebuilding what would be lost. Design in Action alone represented years of accumulated relationships, methodology, and network - none of which transferred to any successor. The window for acting on this recommendation is measured in months.
SPECIFIC ACTIONS
Case vignettes - comparable interventions

Hull City of Culture 2017: Bridge funding from Hull City Council to emerging cultural organisations in the three years prior to City of Culture designation prevented the dissolution of five organisations that were central to the 2017 programme. Post- designation, three achieved sustained funding from Arts Council England. The bridge cost approximately £400,000 over three years; the organisations retained returned an estimated £2.3m in economic activity during the designation year.

Creative Scotland Development Fund: The Development Fund pathway was specifically designed to address the churn cycle by providing multi- year support at a level below Multi- Year Funding but above project grants. Organisations that have transitioned from project funding to Development Fund show, on average, a 40% increase in programme delivery volume within two years. The Recommendation 2 bridge is designed as a feeder into exactly this pathway.

title_page_text: Aberdeen Culture Investment Programme
Introduction

We want Aberdeen to be a city in which the creativity of each of us is valued and given the chance to flourish, and where everyone, regardless of background, has access and opportunity to diverse range of high-quality culture experiences.  We recognise that culture delivers a wide range of social, economic and cultural benefits and are integral to Aberdeen’s prosperity.

The Aberdeen Culture Investment Programme has been designed to support organisations which want to contribute to that goal by delivering sustained programmes of creative or culture activity. It is intended for Aberdeen based organisations which wish to enter into a strategic partnership with Aberdeen City Council (The Council) to deliver culture activities which meet our outcome priorities.
Summary
At a glance
The Aberdeen Culture Investment Programme will offer support to Aberdeen based culture organisations, supporting core costs and programmes of activities from April 2025 onwards.
The Programme will replace The Council’s current funding arrangements for culture activity and introduce a new application process.
The programme is open to Aberdeen based not-for-profit culture organisations. Further information on criteria is provided in the document.
Application will be through a two-stage process, including a registered expression of interest to inform overall demand.
Expression of interest process will open in June 2024; Application process will be open Autumn 2024.

Applicants will be required to meet ‘Following the Public Pound’ criteria, our code of practice requirements for grant giving of public monies. Applicants which cannot satisfy these requirements will not be eligible to progress to full application.
Applicants will need to submit a business plan with their final application, applicants who fail to do so will be excluded.

All applications will be assessed against the published criteria and priorities, the process will include and independent review panel assessment. Panel recommendations will be presented to Council Committee for final approval.
Successful applicants will be notified early 2025 with funding approved at the March Council budget meeting.
Unsuccessful applicants will be provided with support to identify alternative sources of funding and feedback to improve future applications.

While the programme will be competitive, we will commit to ensuring the process is as consistent and transparent as possible by providing clear guidance about how we will assess and how final decisions will be made.  It is therefore essential that applicants take the time to read and fully understand the detail of the guidance before committing to the process.
Culture Review

In 2023 the Council commission a review of its funding and delivery model for culture in order to inform future approaches. The review aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of current Council funding for the delivery of culture initiatives, examining the current funding structure to identify areas for improvement and strategies to optimise the allocation of resources and for more effective impact against Council priorities.

The review identified the current funding model was no longer fit for purpose in reflecting the challenges on public finances but also in respect to support the growth and resilience of the culture sector in Aberdeen.
This document provides guidance on the new framework and how the recommendations from the review have been implemented in the design and delivery of the programme.
Our case for change

The Council invests yearly through its revenue budget and the Common Good Fund on average £12m on culture and heritage, with around £1.5m on average  allocated as grants to external organisations to deliver culture activity. The investment for externally delivered culture activity falls within 3 strands-

Core/ Development Funding:  Investment in Aberdeen’s core independent culture organisations. The list of beneficiaries is historic, and funding has remained flat or reducing on annual basis through Council budget meeting.
Creative Funding: Council open application grant programme to support culture projects delivered in Aberdeen by individuals, not for profit organisations and community groups.
Commissioned Events, festivals, services and activities: Investment in headline events as well as one -off activities and services to support the development of the culture sector.

The need for change was identified through a review of culture delivery and funding, analysis of feedback through the 2024/25 Budget Consultation and the most recent Aberdeen City Population Needs Assessment (PNA).

Consultation has shown there remains significant differences in how ‘culture’ is defined, understood and valued.  Many people are uncomfortable with the label ‘the arts’ and perceive it being for someone else while in reality they may in fact lead very active culture lives and value opportunities to experience and be creative.

While culture is referenced in both Council and regional plans and strategies, currently there is no clear ‘golden thread’ linking objectives and measures, nor specific actions or budgets to support interconnectivity.

The Review has Identified the need for a clearer decision-making framework or criteria for making investment decisions. Who the beneficiaries are off investment and the level received are based on historic arrangements and budget saving decisions over multiple years and not tied to specific measurable outcomes.

title_page_text: From Pinning Stones to Convergence Economy
Mapping of Creative Industries in Aberdeen and Aberdeenshire
Prepared for Aberdeen City Council
April 2026
Iain Bennett and Lynne McCadden, The Fifth Sector
Jon Bains, Obsolete.com
Andy Goodwin and Simon Sprince, Unscrambled.world
Preface: Two studies, conducted twelve years apart, reveal structural similarities

In the winter of 2012–13, François Matarasso travelled across Aberdeenshire speaking to artists, makers, musicians, community organisers and cultural practitioners. He published his findings in 2014 as The Pinning Stones: Culture and Community in Aberdeenshire. It is a precise and honest assessment of a regional creative culture. Its central argument was structural rather than celebratory: that Aberdeenshire’s cultural life was rich, dispersed, self-reliant, largely invisible to policy, and, like the small stones set between the larger granite blocks of a traditional rubble wall, essential to holding everything together. Remove the pinning stones, he wrote, and the mortar cracks faster. The wall looks fine until it doesn’t.
Twelve years later, this research arrives at a different place by a different route and finds, in several important respects, the same thing. And something more.

The methodology is entirely different. Where Matarasso walked and talked, this analysis counted: LinkedIn profiles, company registrations, four tiers of workforce modelling, gross value added calculations, skills comparisons and place-based counterfactuals. Where Matarasso offered a humanist portrait, this report offers an economic audit. The core finding about scale and visibility is structurally identical to his: the region holds a creative economy that is significantly larger, more economically significant, and more strategically important than any official dataset records, and it is hidden in plain view.

But this research finds something Matarasso’s lens could not have seen in 2014: a second structural asset, visible only to an entirely different set of lenses. The simulation and visualisation firms of the Westhill-Dyce corridor and the creative, marketing, and content agencies of Aberdeen City centre each hold precisely what the other commercially lacks. The gap between them is ten miles and the absence of any institution with the mandate to broker a connection. The analysis does not locate a deficit to be remedied, but locates a trading relationship waiting to be made.

The question is why twelve years of intervening policy, strategy and investment have not closed the visibility gap that Matarasso first documented. The answer to that question is also the answer to the Regional Economic Strategy and Local Outcomes Improvement Plan question the commissioners are now asking.
Part One: What this document is and who it is for
1.1 Scope and purpose

This document presents the findings of a comprehensive assessment of the creative economy of Aberdeen City and Aberdeenshire. It is addressed at once to Regional Economic Partnership members and local authority decision-makers; to practitioners and organisations working across the creative, cultural and digital sectors; and to any reader with an interest in how North East Scotland positions itself for sustained economic growth during a period of rapid structural transition.

It draws on original analysis combining official government data, real-time company intelligence and workforce profiling with stakeholder consultation and comparative research. It makes the case for strategic investment grounded in evidence, identifies specific funding opportunities that are available now, and charts the growth pathways available at each level of a creative economy that is larger, more productive and more strategically distinctive than any previous account has recognised.
1.2 Articulating the region’s creative economy
North East Scotland contains three geographically disparate and commercially disconnected creative communities:

The creative, marketing, and content production agencies in the City of Aberdeen hold the narrative capability, client management experience, and commissioning relationships through which major contracts flow.

The second community is the one identified by Matarasso’s 2014 study, The Pinning Stones: Culture and Community in Aberdeenshire: distributed and often disconnected creative practitioners from Banff to Fraserburgh to Montrose and across rural Aberdeenshire,

The third group, a cluster of  digital-technical firms collocated alongside the energy sector in Westhill,  hold world-class technical capability at concentrations far above those of comparable UK cities but have no connection, awareness of or stimulus to connect with the other two groups.

Each is arriving at the limit of what its standalone capability can deliver. Neither currently has a commercial relationship with the other. The separation between them is entirely institutional: a product of geography, sectoral self-identification, and the absence of any mechanism through which a cultural and commercial exchange could be brokered.

This finding sits alongside, and reinforces, the broader finding about scale. The creative economy of North East Scotland accounts for more than 10,700 workers, generates direct gross value added of £582 million, and produces a total annual economic impact of £894 million. Simply acknowledging that there could be greater convergence between those three disparate groups would raise those figures to 12,000 workers, £732 million in GVA and more than £1.1 billion in total economic impact. These figures are not visible in any current policy framework because the measurement tools applied to date were not designed to find them.
1.3 Reframing the strategic question

The tender for this research asked for evidence to demonstrate the position that creative industries should occupy in Regional Economic Strategy. That framing accepts the existing category of creative industries as the unit of analysis. The evidence from both Matarasso’s 2014 analysis and this 2026 research shows that framing is insufficient.

The question the evidence demands is this: what distinctive role can the creative economy of North East Scotland play in sustaining communities through the energy transition, economically, socially, and culturally, in ways that no other region in the United Kingdom is positioned to deliver?
This reframing has four immediate consequences.

It changes the competitive frame: the region does not need to compete with the Central Belt or London in conventional creative industries terms. What the region can offer, and what no other UK city or region can match, is the combination of industrial-scale simulation capability, authentic energy domain knowledge, and the rural-coastal cultural identity that makes technical storytelling about the energy transition credible to international clients and communities.

It changes the measurement framework: if the question is about sustaining communities through transition, then gross value added is one measure but the Local Outcomes Improvement Plan outcome domains become equally important.

title_page_text: Methodology and justification for estimated gross value added
1. Purpose and scope of this chapter

This chapter sets out the complete methodological basis for the estimate of direct Gross Value Added (GVA) of £415.0 million and total economic impact of £633.6 million attributed to the creative industries of Aberdeen and Aberdeenshire. It explains, in sequence, how the business base was established, how the workforce was counted, how GVA was calculated for each tier of that workforce, and how Type II multipliers were applied to derive total economic impact. Each step is documented with sufficient detail to allow independent scrutiny and replication.

The chapter is structured as follows. Section 2 describes the crosswalk methodology used to establish the verified business base. Section 3 explains the four-tier workforce model and the employment intensity adjustments applied to each tier. Section 4 sets out the GVA calculation for each tier and sub-sector. Section 5 explains the Type II multipliers applied to each tier and the derivation of the weighted regional average. Section 6 reconciles the firm-level GVA of £315.4 million with the total direct GVA of £415.0 million. Section 7 addresses the relationship between the excluded shadow economy and the strategic creative core, and the implications of that relationship for regional economic strategy.
2. Establishing the business base: the crosswalk methodology
2.1 The gross registration universe

The starting point for this analysis is a dataset of 1,711 firms provided by The Data City platform, representing every business registered in the Aberdeen and Aberdeenshire area under creative or technology-adjacent Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) codes (The Fifth Sector, 2026c). The Data City uses artificial intelligence to analyse company website content and combine it with Companies House registration data, financial filings, and other public sources, assigning each firm a Real-Time Industrial Classification (RTIC) that reflects its actual trading activity rather than its registered SIC code alone (The Fifth Sector, 2026c).

SIC codes are assigned by firms at the point of registration and are rarely updated thereafter. A software development company registered in 2005 under SIC 62020 (IT consultancy) may have moved entirely into games development or immersive content production in the intervening years without updating its registration. The Data City's RTIC system addresses this by continuously updating its classification based on current website content (The Fifth Sector, 2026c; DCMS, 2013).

Both The Data City platform and the Inter-Departmental Business Register (IDBR) record only firms with a formal legal structure — registered limited companies, limited liability partnerships, and similar entities. Self-employed sole traders and working proprietors without a registered company do not appear in either source, regardless of the sector in which they operate. The business counts in this analysis therefore represent the registered business base only; the self-employed and unregistered workforce is captured separately through the LinkedIn analysis and penetration gap modelling described in Section 3 (ONS, 2024; The Fifth Sector, 2026d).
2.2 The crosswalk filter

To move from 1,711 gross registrations to a verified creative business base, this analysis applies a crosswalk methodology that assesses each firm against a single defining criterion: does the firm derive value primarily from original intellectual property and cultural curation, rather than from the provision of labour hours or technical infrastructure services (The Fifth Sector, 2026c; DCMS, 2013; Bakhshi, Freeman and Higgs, 2013)?

This filter was applied in two passes. The first pass removed the most clearly excludable firms on the basis of four evidenced grounds. The second pass involved detailed spot-checking of firms registered at corporate hub addresses, contractor pattern analysis, and physical footprint verification, which identified a further population of firms that appeared creative on the basis of their SIC code but whose actual activity was industrial utility provision.
The four grounds for exclusion are as follows.

Brass plate registrations are firms using a local accountancy or company formation agent address as their registered office, with no independent evidence of physical operations or staff in the region. Spot checks of 425 firms registered at corporate hubs confirmed that 60% of the statistical data in this category was noise, representing firms with no meaningful local economic footprint (The Fifth Sector, 2026c).

Personal service companies are firms established as tax-efficient vehicles for individual IT contractors working in the energy sector. These firms are registered under creative or technology SIC codes but their sole economic function is to invoice for the labour of a single individual on energy sector projects. Analysis identified that 40% of entities in the technology-adjacent SIC codes followed this contractor pattern (The Fifth Sector, 2026c).
Nominee registrations are firms with no local staff, no studio or office footprint, and no evidence of trading activity, accounting for 25% of the excluded population (The Fifth Sector, 2026c).

Industrial utility firms are firms whose primary output is technical infrastructure support for the energy sector — reservoir telemetry, technical safety manual translation, offshore project management, asset integrity management — rather than creative content, products or experiences. These firms are more accurately understood as part of the energy services cluster than the creative economy (The Fifth Sector, 2026c; DCMS, 2013).
2.3 The resulting business populations
Application of the crosswalk filter produces the following business populations.
Table 1: Business population after crosswalk
Source: The Fifth Sector (2026c); The Fifth Sector (2026i); The Fifth Sector (2026j)

The active creative core of 852 firms includes 840 firms mapped to the nine DCMS creative industries sub-sectors and 12 firms in the cultural sector — covering historical sites, music retail, and instrument manufacture — that fall outside the strict DCMS creative industries definition but are integral to the regional creative ecosystem (The Fifth Sector, 2026a; DCMS, 2013).
2.4 Comparison with the official administrative baseline

The Inter-Departmental Business Register provides the official administrative count of creative businesses. Comparison between the IDBR 2025 figures and the crosswalk results illustrates both the limitations of administrative data and the value of the crosswalk approach.
Table 2: Comparison of IDBR 2025 counts with crosswalk results by DCMS sub-sector
Source: ONS (2024); The Fifth Sector (2026a); The Fifth Sector (2026c)

Note: The IDBR total of 1,005 and the crosswalk gross registration total of 1,711 are not directly comparable because The Data City captures a wider range of technology-adjacent SIC codes than the IDBR creative industries classification. The excluded total of 860 in this table reflects rounding in the sub-sector breakdown; the authoritative excluded total is 859 firms.

The comparison reveals two systematic distortions in the administrative data. First, the IDBR significantly overcounts IT, software and computer services (435 firms) because it includes energy technical utilities and personal service companies registered under SIC 62020. The crosswalk reduces this to 130 verified creative technology firms. Second, the IDBR count for music, performing and visual arts (75 firms) understates the verified active firm count of 200 because it misses the high proportion of micro-enterprises and sole director companies in this sub-sector — small production companies, artist-led studios, and independent music businesses — that are registered at Companies House but fall below the IDBR's PAYE threshold. It should be noted that this discrepancy reflects the prevalence of registered micro-companies in these sub-sectors, not the presence of unregistered sole traders, who do not appear in either the IDBR or The Data City data (The Fifth Sector, 2026a; The Fifth Sector, 2026c).

title_page_text: GVA Attribution Methodology
How we avoid over-counting GVA from non-creative firms in the convergence economy analysis
NES Creative Industries Sector Mapping Research  ·  Aberdeen City Council  ·  May 2026
When we count the creative economy, we face two distinct risks.

The first is under-counting: missing firms whose creative-digital work is invisible in standard SIC code statistics. The Westhill-Dyce and adjacent clusters address this — they bring non-CCI firms into the analysis because their actual trading activity involves simulation, 3D visualisation, geospatial analytics, and digital twin development.

The second is over-counting: attributing the full GVA of a large firm to the creative economy when creative-digital work is only a fraction of that firm's total activity. A 647-person marine engineering company with £22 million in GVA and a weak RTIC convergence signal should not contribute its entire GVA to the creative economy count.
The attribution methodology described in this document solves the second problem without undermining the first.
We use two independent signals from the foresight-report-337 dataset, produced by Data City. They use different evidence and act as cross-checks on each other.
Signal 1 — SIC code mix ratio (the structural proxy)
What it is

The SIC (Standard Industrial Classification) code is the legal category a company registers with Companies House to describe its business. Most companies register one or two SIC codes. Some register several — particularly firms that operate across creative and non-creative sectors.
How we use it

For each firm, we count how many of its registered SIC codes fall within the DCMS creative industries definition (the same definition used throughout the base four-tier model), and how many fall outside it. The ratio of CCI SIC codes to total SIC codes gives us a simple structural measure of what fraction of the firm's registered activity is creative.
What this signal does well
It is objective and verifiable — SIC codes are Companies House public record.
It correctly excludes large non-creative firms (Firm C above) even if they have some creative-digital RTIC signal.
It produces the most conservative (lowest) GVA attribution, acting as a floor.
What this signal does less well

It can be overly conservative: Firm C in the example above has 647 employees and carries Robotics and Marine RTICs — its sim/vis work is real, but because it registered under engineering SIC codes only, Method 1 gives it zero attribution.

SIC codes describe what a company legally registered to do, not necessarily what it currently does. A firm that began as an oil-and-gas consultancy but now derives 30% of revenue from simulation visualisation may still carry only engineering SIC codes.
Signal 2 —Convergence Score (the trading evidence proxy)
What it is

The Convergence Score is a proprietary score (ranging from 0 to 1) that we calculate for every firm in the dataset using a mixture of RTICs and text descriptors derived from The Data City. It combines four types of evidence:
The firm's RTIC (Real-Time Industrial Classification) — based on what its website says it does today, not what SIC code it registered under.
The presence of convergence-relevant terms in its website text (simulation, visualisation, digital twins, geospatial, immersive, animation, VFX, etc.).
How strongly those terms appear: a firm whose homepage leads with "digital twin solutions for offshore assets" scores higher than one where "simulation" appears once in a services list.
The mix of SIC codes: a firm with both CCI and engineering SIC codes scores differently from one with only engineering codes.
How to interpret the score
