title_page_text: GVA Attribution Methodology
How we calculate the creative-digital proportion of GVA from non-CCI adjacent firms
NES Creative Industries Sector Mapping Research  ·  Aberdeen City Council  ·  May 2026

The four clusters identified in the convergence economy analysis include non-CCI adjacent firms — companies registered under engineering, software, robotics, and data infrastructure SIC codes rather than creative industries codes. These firms are included because their actual trading activity, as revealed by RTIC analysis and website content, involves work at the intersection of technical and creative disciplines.

Including them raises a practical problem. When we take the full GVA of a large engineering or marine technology company and count it toward the creative economy, we are almost certainly overstating the creative contribution. A company with 200 engineers and £20 million in GVA that also produces some data visualisation work for offshore clients should not have its entire £20 million counted as creative-economy output.

The attribution methodology described in this document applies a structured discount to each firm's GVA based on two evidence signals, so that only the proportion of activity with genuine creative-digital relevance is counted. The result is a defensible range, not a single precise figure.
Before describing the method, it is important to distinguish two separate questions that are easy to confuse.
This document is primarily concerned with Question 2. The attribution method applies only to Tier B firms.
Two independent evidence signals are combined to produce the attribution. They use different types of data and serve as cross-checks on each other.
Signal 1 — SIC code mix (the structural signal)

The SIC (Standard Industrial Classification) code is what a company registers at Companies House to describe its legal business type. Most companies register between one and four SIC codes. We count how many of a firm's registered SIC codes fall within the DCMS creative industries definition and how many do not. The ratio of CCI codes to total codes gives a simple structural measure of the firm's registered creative activity.

Important caveat: SIC 61 (Telecommunications) is excluded from the CCI count and from the convergence analysis entirely. Telecommunications is a utility infrastructure service — it supplies the pipes through which digital content travels — rather than an indicator of creative or convergence activity. A firm whose only SIC code is SIC 61 is excluded from the Tier B attribution regardless of any RTIC signal.
Signal 2 — Convergence score (the trading evidence signal)
The convergence score is a composite indicator derived by The Fifth Sector from data obtained through The Data City. It draws on three sources of evidence:
The firm's RTIC (Real-Time Industrial Classification) — a classification based on what its website says it currently does, independent of its registered SIC codes.

The presence and strength of convergence-relevant terms in the firm's website text: simulation, visualisation, digital twin, geospatial, immersive, animation, VFX, and related terms. A firm whose homepage leads with "digital twin solutions" scores higher than one where "simulation" appears once in a subsidiary services page.
The SIC mix: a firm with both CCI and non-CCI SIC codes and strong website text receives a higher score than one with only the website text signal.

The convergence score runs from 0 to 1. Unlike a continuous multiplier, the attribution framework uses the score to assign firms to one of four defined cases, each with a fixed attribution rate. This makes the approach more transparent and less sensitive to small differences in scores at the margins.
Every Tier B firm with GVA data is assigned to one of five cases based on its CCI SIC ratio and convergence score. The attribution rate for each case is fixed.
Why fixed rates rather than a continuous multiplier?

A continuous method (GVA × convergence score for each firm) appears more precise but is misleading. The convergence score varies within narrow ranges that do not carry reliable analytical meaning at the individual firm level. A firm scoring 0.61 and one scoring 0.68 are not meaningfully different. The five-case framework is transparent, auditable, and clearly communicates the logic of each decision without false precision.

The following examples are drawn from the actual foresight-337 dataset. They are anonymised by description rather than name. All GVA figures are Companies House estimates, not audited accounts. They are chosen specifically because they are small, representative firms — not the large-GVA outliers that dominate aggregate totals.

title_page_text: From Pinning Stones to Convergence Economy
Mapping of Creative Industries in Aberdeen and Aberdeenshire
Prepared for Aberdeen City Council
April 2026
Iain Bennett and Lynne McCadden, The Fifth Sector
Jon Bains, Obsolete.com
Andy Goodwin and Simon Sprince, Unscrambled.world
Preface: Two studies, conducted twelve years apart, reveal structural similarities

In the winter of 2012–13, François Matarasso travelled across Aberdeenshire speaking to artists, makers, musicians, community organisers and cultural practitioners. He published his findings in 2014 as The Pinning Stones: Culture and Community in Aberdeenshire. It is a precise and honest assessment of a regional creative culture. Its central argument was structural rather than celebratory: that Aberdeenshire’s cultural life was rich, dispersed, self-reliant, largely invisible to policy, and, like the small stones set between the larger granite blocks of a traditional rubble wall, essential to holding everything together. Remove the pinning stones, he wrote, and the mortar cracks faster. The wall looks fine until it doesn’t.
Twelve years later, this research arrives at a different place by a different route and finds, in several important respects, the same thing. And something more.

The methodology is entirely different. Where Matarasso walked and talked, this analysis counted: LinkedIn profiles, company registrations, four tiers of workforce modelling, gross value added calculations, skills comparisons and place-based counterfactuals. Where Matarasso offered a humanist portrait, this report offers an economic audit. The core finding about scale and visibility is structurally identical to his: the region holds a creative economy that is significantly larger, more economically significant, and more strategically important than any official dataset records, and it is hidden in plain view.

But this research finds something Matarasso’s lens could not have seen in 2014: a second structural asset, visible only to an entirely different set of lenses. The simulation and visualisation firms of the Westhill-Dyce corridor and the creative, marketing, and content agencies of Aberdeen City centre each hold precisely what the other commercially lacks. The gap between them is ten miles and the absence of any institution with the mandate to broker a connection. The analysis does not locate a deficit to be remedied, but locates a trading relationship waiting to be made.

The question is why twelve years of intervening policy, strategy and investment have not closed the visibility gap that Matarasso first documented. The answer to that question is also the answer to the Regional Economic Strategy and Local Outcomes Improvement Plan question the commissioners are now asking.
Part One: What this document is and who it is for
1.1 Scope and purpose

This document presents the findings of a comprehensive assessment of the creative economy of Aberdeen City and Aberdeenshire. It is addressed at once to Regional Economic Partnership members and local authority decision-makers; to practitioners and organisations working across the creative, cultural and digital sectors; and to any reader with an interest in how North East Scotland positions itself for sustained economic growth during a period of rapid structural transition.

It draws on original analysis combining official government data, real-time company intelligence and workforce profiling with stakeholder consultation and comparative research. It makes the case for strategic investment grounded in evidence, identifies specific funding opportunities that are available now, and charts the growth pathways available at each level of a creative economy that is larger, more productive and more strategically distinctive than any previous account has recognised.
1.2 Articulating the region’s creative economy
North East Scotland contains three geographically disparate and commercially disconnected creative communities:

The creative, marketing, and content production agencies in the City of Aberdeen hold the narrative capability, client management experience, and commissioning relationships through which major contracts flow.

The second community is the one identified by Matarasso’s 2014 study, The Pinning Stones: Culture and Community in Aberdeenshire: distributed and often disconnected creative practitioners from Banff to Fraserburgh to Montrose and across rural Aberdeenshire,

The third group, a cluster of  digital-technical firms collocated alongside the energy sector in Westhill,  hold world-class technical capability at concentrations far above those of comparable UK cities but have no connection, awareness of or stimulus to connect with the other two groups.

Each is arriving at the limit of what its standalone capability can deliver. Neither currently has a commercial relationship with the other. The separation between them is entirely institutional: a product of geography, sectoral self-identification, and the absence of any mechanism through which a cultural and commercial exchange could be brokered.

This finding sits alongside, and reinforces, the broader finding about scale. The creative economy of North East Scotland accounts for more than 10,700 workers, generates direct gross value added of £582 million, and produces a total annual economic impact of £894 million. Simply acknowledging that there could be greater convergence between those three disparate groups would raise those figures to 12,000 workers, £732 million in GVA and more than £1.1 billion in total economic impact. These figures are not visible in any current policy framework because the measurement tools applied to date were not designed to find them.
1.3 Reframing the strategic question

The tender for this research asked for evidence to demonstrate the position that creative industries should occupy in Regional Economic Strategy. That framing accepts the existing category of creative industries as the unit of analysis. The evidence from both Matarasso’s 2014 analysis and this 2026 research shows that framing is insufficient.

The question the evidence demands is this: what distinctive role can the creative economy of North East Scotland play in sustaining communities through the energy transition, economically, socially, and culturally, in ways that no other region in the United Kingdom is positioned to deliver?
This reframing has four immediate consequences.

It changes the competitive frame: the region does not need to compete with the Central Belt or London in conventional creative industries terms. What the region can offer, and what no other UK city or region can match, is the combination of industrial-scale simulation capability, authentic energy domain knowledge, and the rural-coastal cultural identity that makes technical storytelling about the energy transition credible to international clients and communities.

It changes the measurement framework: if the question is about sustaining communities through transition, then gross value added is one measure but the Local Outcomes Improvement Plan outcome domains become equally important.

title_page_text: FORESIGHT / REPORT 337 / NE SCOTLAND
Aberdeen's Creative Economy: What the Company Data Actually Shows
Structural synthesis: company SIC analysis, IP sensitivity framework, LinkedIn workforce mapping, automation exposure, and 2035 strategic read. Sources distinguished throughout.
■  FRAMEWORK
Four Types of Incorporation — Defined by IP Sensitivity and Workflow Position
Not all incorporated micro-entities are the same thing. The SIC code distribution, workflow position, and employment structure differ sharply by why the company exists.

These four types face completely different automation exposure, different relationships to ONS-invisible workforce, and require different strategic interventions. Treating them as one category — 'CCI micro-entities' — produces analysis wrong in every direction.
■  CORRECTION 01
The 2025 Formation Spike Is Predominantly Type 1, Not Type 3
Earlier analysis described 251 new CCI companies in 2025 as primarily advertising and design freelancers incorporating under automation pressure. The SIC data contradicts this directly.

T3 (advertising/design execution) formed 19 companies in 2025 — lower than 2020 and a declining share. Type 1 is 127 of 251 (51%). The acceleration is primarily formalisation responding to IP client requirements.  The T4 spike (27 in 2025 vs 2–3 historically) is not straightforwardly 'professional legitimacy' incorporation. It may equally represent artists and performers coming together to form studios and independent production companies — a defensive response to arts budget cuts and Council funding uncertainty. Formal structures are increasingly required to access grant funding. This may be 'huddling together for warmth' as much as expansive entrepreneurialism.
Source: SortableIncorporationDate, CCI Companies sheet, Report 337. Classified by primary SIC code.
■  CORRECTION 02
The 981 Micro-Entities Are Not Post-Production Contractors — They Are Four Different Populations
Earlier analysis characterised the micro-entity layer as primarily screen post-production contractors. That was built on 19 classified companies (2%) and was wrong.
Source: CCI Companies sheet, Report 337. Classified by primary SIC code.
■  CORRECTION 03
The ONS-Invisible Workforce Is Real — But It Cannot Exist in Type 1 Work

The workforce not captured in ONS/BRES data is substantial but concentrated in specific IP types. Note: 'invisible' in this document means invisible to ONS/BRES. A separate and more extreme category — those with no professional online presence of any kind — maps to Tier 4 Shared Utility Workers in the tier structure used elsewhere in this analysis.
■  EVIDENCE
LinkedIn Data Confirms the Scale — Creative Workers Not Captured in ONS/BRES

LinkedIn workforce mapping across NE Scotland creative supply chains, cross-referenced against BRES 2024. Tier labels updated: Cultural Core, Creative Employees, Creative Freelancers, Shared Utility Workers.
Tier Structure — What BRES Can and Cannot See

Tier 4 Shared Utility Workers are doubly invisible: not in ONS/BRES records and not in LinkedIn or any other professional data source. This is the most extreme information gap — the workforce that no current intelligence system, including this one, can see.
Source: NE Scotland LinkedIn workforce mapping 2026. BRES 2024 Aberdeen City and Aberdeenshire.
BRES vs LinkedIn Multiplier by DCMS Sector
Source: BRES 2024 (Aberdeen City + Aberdeenshire combined). LinkedIn NE Scotland creative workforce mapping 2026.
Freelance and Contractor Share by Creative Supply Chain Category
Total is 8,455 (cleaned dataset including historical sites and museums). Earlier tables showing 8,155 omitted historical sites and museums and were incorrect.

title_page_text: Mapping of creative industries in Aberdeen and Aberdeenshire
Prepared for Aberdeen City Council
May 2026
Iain Bennett and Lynne McCadden, The Fifth Sector
Jon Bains, Obsolete.com
Andy Goodwin and Simon Sprince, Unscrambled.world
Preface: Two studies, twelve years apart

In the winter of 2012-13, Francois Matarasso travelled across Aberdeenshire speaking to artists, makers, musicians, community organisers and cultural practitioners. He published his findings in 2014 as The Pinning Stones: Culture and Community in Aberdeenshire. It is a precise and honest assessment of a regional creative culture. Its central argument was structural rather than celebratory: that Aberdeenshire's cultural life was rich, dispersed, self-reliant, largely invisible to policy, and, like the small stones set between the larger granite blocks of a traditional rubble wall, essential to holding everything together. Remove the pinning stones, he wrote, and the mortar cracks faster. The wall looks fine until it doesn't.
Twelve years later, this research arrives at a different place by a different route and finds, in several important respects, the same thing. And something more.

The methodology is entirely different. Where Matarasso walked and talked, this analysis counted: LinkedIn profiles, company registrations, four tiers of workforce modelling, gross value added calculations, skills comparisons and place-based counterfactuals. Where Matarasso offered a humanist portrait, this report offers an economic audit. The core finding about scale and visibility is structurally identical to his: the region holds a creative economy that is significantly larger, more economically significant, and more strategically important than any official dataset records, and it is hidden in plain view.

But this research finds something Matarasso's lens could not have seen in 2014: a separate convergence opportunity. Technical firms with transferable creative-digital capability and creative firms with energy-sector client relationships operate alongside one another, but often unaware of each other. A strategic focus on turning that coexistence into effective cooperation could unlock opportunities to grow the region's creative economy in ways that reinforce a just transition from dependence on fossil fuels. The report puts forward ways to market test and exploit those nascent synergies.

The report casts new light on these opportunities, as well as those presented by the city's creative core and the distinctive strengths of cultural life in the region's urban and coastal districts. It seeks to close the visibility gap that Matarasso first documented; and in doing so, it looks to demonstrate how the creative economy can be identified as a critical success factor in both Regional Economic Strategy and the Local Outcomes Improvement Plan.
Part one: What this document is and who it is for
1.1 Scope and purpose

This document presents the findings of a comprehensive assessment of the creative economy of Aberdeen City and Aberdeenshire. It is addressed at once to Regional Economic Partnership members and local authority decision-makers; to practitioners and organisations working across the creative, cultural and digital sectors; and to any reader with an interest in how North East Scotland positions itself for sustained economic growth during a period of rapid structural transition.

It draws on original analysis combining official government data, real-time company intelligence and workforce profiling with stakeholder consultation and comparative research. It makes the case for strategic investment grounded in evidence, identifies specific funding opportunities that are available now, and charts the growth pathways available at each level of a creative economy that is larger, more productive and more strategically distinctive than any previous account has recognised.
1.2 Articulating the region's creative economy
North East Scotland contains three geographically dispersed and commercially disconnected creative communities:
City-centre creative, marketing and content production agencies hold narrative capability, client management experience and commissioning relationships.
Rural and coastal creative practitioners operate across Aberdeenshire and the north-east coast, often outside registered business structures.

Technical firms with transferable creative-digital capability sit across the four convergence geographies identified in Part Four: city centre; a corridor running from Westhill to Dyce; south Aberdeen and Stonehaven; and Inverurie and Kintore.

Each community has capability that matters to the region's future creative economy. The evidence shows that the base creative economy is larger than official datasets record: 10,490 workers, 7,715 FTE, £453 million in direct GVA and £675 million in total economic impact. It does not yet prove that these communities are already selling into the same markets, or that demand for new forms of creative experience is large enough to support a new growth programme; it identifies potential growth that requires market testing.
1.3 Strategic significance of creative industries in North East Scotland

The evidence gathered here points to the distinctive role that the creative economy of North East Scotland can play in sustaining communities through the energy transition, economically, socially, and culturally, in ways that no other region in the United Kingdom is positioned to deliver.
The significance of the creative economy exists across four dimensions:

The region has distinctive strengths: it does not need to compete with the Central Belt or London in conventional creative industries terms. What the region can offer, and what no other UK city or region can match, is the combination of industrial-scale simulation capability, authentic energy domain knowledge, and the rural-coastal cultural identity that makes technical storytelling about the energy transition credible to international clients and communities.

Recognising the gross value added contribution made by creative industries and how to increase that is significant: but if the question is about sustaining communities through transition, strategy for the sector needs to recognise that the Local Outcomes Improvement Plan outcome domains are equally important.

The evidence contradicts a false binary choice between investment in digital sectors and creative industries, and argues that the right approach is a sequenced strategy that addresses different populations at different timescales.

Addressing those combined opportunities calls for a change to current institutional governance: no existing body is currently configured to provide solutions that respond to the evidence presented in this research, and the answer is a new mandate rather than a new agency.

title_page_text: Mapping the Creative Industries in Aberdeen and Aberdeenshire
Executive Summary
Background to the research

This research was commissioned by Aberdeen City Council to map the creative industries in Aberdeen and Aberdeenshire. The commissioners asked for a clear evidence base to inform the place of creative industries within the Regional Economic Strategy, support for future investment decisions, identification of opportunities for sector development, and practical recommendations for local authorities and regional partners. The research operates as both an economic mapping exercise and a strategic development study. It assesses the scale, composition and value of the creative economy; examines the relationships between creative, cultural, digital and energy-transition capabilities; and sets out actions for councils, regional agencies, funders, education providers and sector organisations.

Between October 2025 and April 2026, the research team conducted interviews with stakeholders from policy, education, cultural and creative sector organisations, individual artists and support networks. Four in-person workshops in Aberdeen in November 2025 brought together practitioners, anchor organisations, local authority officers and representatives of national agencies.

The interviews and workshops arrived at the same conclusions as the desk research. The data showed a sector weighted towards freelance and micro-enterprise activity, lacking the deep commercial middle ground found in comparable regions. Workshop participants described the same view from the sector's perspective: the freelance tier is "hidden, hungry, struggling and undervalued" (AAMD_002). The fact that the two lines of evidence converge on the same structural conclusion gives confidence in both sets of findings.
What the data reveals and why this is different from national statistics

National statistics measure employment in registered businesses. Applied to North East Scotland's creative economy, that approach identifies just under 5,000 employees, including between 1,400 and 1,600  generic IT consultants. Self-employed and freelance practitioners do not appear in it at all. In a sector where over 90% of registered creative enterprises employ fewer than ten people and more than a third of practitioners are freelance, the exclusion of self-employed workers is a structural flaw in the measurement, not a small rounding error.

This research works across three layers of evidence: official administrative data from BRES and IDBR; real-time analysis of what companies are actually doing, derived from their website content, through The Data City platform; and LinkedIn workforce profiling, treated as a large-scale pre-filled occupational survey. The LinkedIn analysis identified more than 8,400 unique creative profiles among North East Scotland residents, including more than 1,500 additional employees and 3,280 self-employed and freelance workers not captured in official statistics.

The combined picture is substantially larger than any previous account of this economy. The region holds 10,490 creative workers, generating £453 million in direct GVA and £675 million in total economic impact. These figures are not visible in any current policy framework because the measurement tools previously applied were not designed to find them.
What a comparison with the UK national picture and other areas highlights as the strengths of NES's creative economy
North East Scotland's creative economy has two structural characteristics that are unusual in the UK context and that are not the result of any regional or national creative economy policy.

The first is the nature and depth of its technical capability. The research found far higher levels of simulation, visualisation and engineering-grade digital skills in the regional workforce than those found in other UK regions. The industrial origin of these skills matters: they were generated and sustained by fifty years of demand for safety-critical offshore operations. As a result, those skills are more deeply embedded and more resistant to displacement than capability built through any policy programme. They can be translated into markets for renewable energy as the oil and gas sector declines, and they open up new markets for immersive and real-time entertainment in film, games, live events and new kinds of visitor experience.

The second is the character of the rural and coastal cultural sector. Hundreds of independent artists, makers and musicians have built their own studio communities, open studio networks and retail platforms, generating real commercial output that official statistics miss entirely. This is a structural feature specific to a region with deep craft and cultural traditions embedded in dispersed rural and coastal communities. Creative economies of this type are rare in UK city-regions.
Both structural conditions create distinct commercial opportunities that a region without them cannot readily acquire. The strategies in this report exist to make that opportunity reachable.
What a comparison with the UK national picture and other areas highlights as the weaknesses of NES's creative economy

The distinctive structure that creates North East Scotland's strengths also contains a built-in limitation: two commercially valuable parts of the economy have developed in parallel without yet finding a way to work together.

There is a cohort of technical and engineering firms, many of them working in energy and adjacent sectors, that hold capabilities in simulation and 3D visualisation technologies that content, entertainment and communications markets would pay a premium for. The city-centre creative agencies hold creative strategy, storytelling and production capability that energy-domain and transition communications clients need. Each holds what the other needs to reach higher-value markets.

The skills the region lacks are precisely the bridging skills that would allow those two halves to connect: virtual production, data storytelling and real-time rendering. Their absence is measurable in both the quantitative and qualitative evidence and it is the direct consequence of the separation between the technical and creative economies.

Graduates leaving the region's universities with the technical and creative skills this region needs are more likely to pursue a career in other parts of Scotland, the rest of the UK and overseas because the distinctive career that combining creative practice with the region's simulation and visualisation skills could support has never been made clear to them at the point when they decide whether to stay or go. Closing the creative-digital gap could improve retention rates and, in the medium term, encourage more alumni currently working elsewhere to return.
What are the drivers of the resulting distinctive sector structure?

The sector currently contains three groups of people and organisations, each playing a distinct role. Cultural anchor institutions, including museums, galleries, performing arts venues and heritage bodies, sustain the public programming, skills pipeline and institutional credibility on which the rest of the sector depends. Commercial creative and digital SMEs generate the revenue, employment and supply chain connections that give the sector its economic weight. Rural and coastal artists, makers and musicians carry the distinctive character of the cultural offer. Doric language, fishing and farming tradition, and the visual and musical culture of the north-east coast give the region's creative work a character that external markets recognise as distinctively their own. That heritage spans four millennia and is still active in the work being made today.

Outside Aberdeen city centre, practitioners are spread across a wide rural and coastal area, with little physical or networking infrastructure to connect them. Because they are spread across such a wide area, those connections have never had the chance to form naturally. That is why investment in shared space, meeting and event facilities and mobile programming would return more here than in an economy where some of that already exists.

The research identified three opportunities for growth. The first is the convergence between creative practice and the technical skill base generated by fifty years of offshore energy. The per-capita concentration of simulation and visualisation skills in the workforce runs at 3.5 times the rate found in Nottingham, the most comparable UK city-region for this analysis, and we found nothing equivalent in any other comparable UK city-region we have studied. Those skills transfer directly into high-value screen, games, immersive and technical production, but the exchange of creative and technical knowledge that would make it happen has not yet developed. The second opportunity is cross-sector and interdisciplinary working, which the dispersed geography of the sector currently works against. The third is formal and informal networking to share knowledge, skills and access to domestic and export markets, which many practitioners currently lack. The strategies set out in this report address all three.
Are we double-counting digital sector activity in IT and software?
No; read together, this report and the earlier report from Opportunity North East into the Digital Tech sector clarify the relationship between the regional technology base and the creative economy.

The IT and software capacity in the region falls into three broad categories: firms whose activity belongs exclusively to the digital technology sectors the ONE report covers; firms providing IT services and infrastructure that support both digital and creative businesses; and firms offering creative-digital services to both the creative economy and other sectors. The crosswalk methodology applied in this report distinguishes between them, applying a conservative treatment that retains only firms with confirmed creative-digital activity for analysis and excludes generic IT infrastructure, systems integration and energy-sector support from the headline counts of businesses, employment and GVA. The simulation and visualisation crossover with the energy sector is recognised and its relationship to the creative economy articulated; but its employment and outputs are not counted toward the creative economy.
How a four-tier model reconciles cultural and creative economy structures

Most economic assessments of the creative sector measure businesses, employment and GVA and leave the social and cultural connections between institutions, firms, freelancers and independent practitioners unrecorded. This research uses a four-tier model to reflect and reconcile those relationships, because the structural connections between inter-related and inter-dependent cultural and creative activities matter to the economic argument as much as the headline figures. Retaining the perspective of cultural institutions and of rural and coastal artists makes culture central to the creative economy, not a supplement to it.

The Tier 1 institutions, the museums, galleries, theatres and performing arts venues, concentrated in Aberdeen city but also found in towns across the Shire, are economic anchors as well as cultural ones. They sustain creative employment directly, draw audiences whose spending supports the wider local economy, and form a significant part of the region's visitor offer. They give the sector its public presence, its relationship with audiences, and the institutional continuity that allows the commercial tiers to operate in a place with a visible, functioning cultural life.

The creative workforce Foresight cannot currently see
What the gap is, why it matters, and how we plan to close it
The problem
When Foresight analyses a region's creative industries, it draws on two main data sources: official employment statistics
(BRES, the Business Register and Employment Survey) and Lightcast job posting data. Both of these share a
fundamental characteristic: they only record activity that flows through formal employment channels. A company posts a
job, it shows up in Lightcast. A company pays PAYE employees, they show up in BRES.
This works reasonably well for industries where most people are full-time employees of registered businesses. It does not
work for the creative industries, where the majority of practitioners are freelancers, self-employed contractors, or informal
workers who never appear on any payroll. In film production, for instance, the core permanent team of a production
company might be three or four people. The actual crew that makes a film is sixty people hired specifically for that project.
BRES records four. The sixty are invisible.
Across the creative industries as a whole this invisibility is not marginal. The best available evidence suggests that official
statistics capture somewhere between 30 and 60 percent of the actual creative workforce depending on the sub-sector. In
music, arts, and crafts the undercounting is severe. In tech and design it is less bad. On average, the real workforce is
roughly twice the size of what official numbers show.
The current consequence for Foresight is straightforward: when LinkedIn data is sparse in a region (which is often), the
system defaults the hidden workforce to zero. It calculates economic impact using a single multiplier applied to the

Executive Summary
Background to the research

This research was commissioned by Aberdeen City Council to map the creative industries in Aberdeen and Aberdeenshire. The commissioners asked for a clear evidence base to inform the place of creative industries within the Regional Economic Strategy, support for future investment decisions, identification of opportunities for sector development, and practical recommendations for local authorities and regional partners. The research operates as both an economic mapping exercise and a strategic development study. It assesses the scale, composition and value of the creative economy; examines the relationships between creative, cultural, digital and energy-transition capabilities; and sets out actions for councils, regional agencies, funders, education providers and sector organisations.
What the data reveals and why this is different from national statistics

National statistics measure employment in registered businesses. Applied to North East Scotland's creative economy, that approach identifies just under 5,000 employees, including between 1,400 and 1,600  generic IT consultants. Self-employed and freelance practitioners do not appear in it at all. In a sector where over 90% of registered creative enterprises employ fewer than ten people and more than a third of practitioners are freelance, the exclusion of self-employed workers is a structural flaw in the measurement, not a small rounding error.

This research works across three layers of evidence: official administrative data from BRES and IDBR; real-time analysis of what companies are actually doing, derived from their website content, through The Data City platform; and LinkedIn workforce profiling, treated as a large-scale pre-filled occupational survey. The LinkedIn analysis identified more than 8,400 unique creative profiles among North East Scotland residents, including more than 1,500 additional employees and 3,280 self-employed and freelance workers not captured in official statistics.

The combined picture is substantially larger than any previous account of this economy. The region holds 10,490 creative workers, generating £453 million in direct GVA and £675 million in total economic impact. These figures are not visible in any current policy framework because the measurement tools previously applied were not designed to find them.

title_page_text: POLICY PLAYBOOK
North East Scotland Creative Industries Strategy
Five costed, sequenced and accountable recommendations
Appendix to: From Pinning Stones to a Convergence Economy
How to use this document
This Policy Playbook translates the five strategic recommendations of the main report into a programme management instrument. Each recommendation is presented with:
The specific actions required (not just the intent)
The lead body and delivery partners
A costed range broken down by year
A delivery timeline in 6–12–24-month bands
Measurable KPIs against which progress can be reported
Key risks and dependencies that could delay or prevent delivery.

The Playbook is designed to be extracted from the main report and used as a standalone working document by the Joint Creative Economy Board (Recommendation 2), by programme officers in both local authorities, and by Creative Scotland and Scottish Enterprise in their supporting roles. It is also the submission artefact requested by Scottish Government as evidence of a costed, actionable plan.

Recommendations are sequenced by strategic priority. Recommendation 1 (CoSTAR bid) carries the firmest external deadline – the June 2026 Innovate UK call confirmation – and active bid preparation is required now. Recommendation 4 ('Breaking the churn cycle') has the most urgent delivery window: some connective organisations are at immediate risk of dissolution and the window for intervention is measured in months, not years. Recommendation 2 (governance) is the enabling condition for the others to function as a coherent programme.
Master delivery sequence
The table below shows the delivery timeline for all five recommendations across a four-year implementation horizon. Shading indicates when each recommendation is in active delivery.
Recommendation 1  Advance a joint CoSTAR bid
Aberdeen–Dundee Creative Technology Corridor: positioning Aberdeen's simulation surplus for UKRI cluster investment
Rationale and opportunity

UKRI's CoSTAR (Convergent screen technologies and performance in realtime) programme represents the largest available UK investment in creative industries convergence. Aberdeen's typological differentiation – energy-creative convergence in an oil transition economy, with a simulation surplus at 3.5 times the per capita concentration of comparable UK city-regions – is a compelling case for CoSTAR cluster investment that Edinburgh, Glasgow, and London cannot replicate. Within the headline creative economy, the region has 920 Tier 2 registered creative businesses generating £226 million in direct Tier 2 GVA; around the headline creative economy sits a further pure_adjacent tier of around 25 firms with confirmed creative-technical crossover activity – entirely invisible in previous regional economic assessments – and around 90 Group B firms in the energy services and engineering sectors whose simulation and visualisation capabilities are directly contiguous with creative technology markets. This is precisely the evidence base a CoSTAR bid can deploy.

CoSTAR Realtime Lab (led by Abertay University), based at Water's Edge, Dundee, is a real-time virtual production R&D lab for games, film, animation and immersive media that combines game-engine, motion-capture and real-time graphics technologies to support industry-led R&D, prototyping and commercialisation in the creative tech sector. A satellite lab in Aberdeen would bring North East Scotland's outstanding capability and capacity in simulation and 3D visualisation, creating a corridor with the profile and diverse market demand to compete for investment at a scale that neither city could achieve individually.

A call for proposals for CoSTAR satellite labs is expected to be announced in June 2026; a bid must be in active preparation now. This is the recommendation with the largest potential financial return: a successful CoSTAR award of up to £5 million would fund the cluster development infrastructure, CPD programme delivery, and convergence firm connectivity programme that the strategies in Part Nine and recommendations in Part Ten of the main report require.
SPECIFIC ACTIONS
Case vignettes – comparable interventions

The School of Informatics at University of Edinburgh: This offers a direct precedent for pan-regional cooperation within CoSTAR. The School of Informatics is a core CoSTAR Realtime Lab partner supplying AI/ML and generative-AI research expertise, researchers (including postdocs), and data-analytics capability; it helps host the Edinburgh site (with Edinburgh College of Art/Design Informatics) and contributes to R&D in real-time graphics, content generation, motion capture/animation and production pipelines.

South of Scotland CreaTech Fund: The most directly comparable Scottish precedent, providing investment in creative technology businesses in a region transitioning from traditional industries. Early-stage firms receiving support showed average revenue growth of 34% in the first two years. The fund established the precedent of treating creative technology as economic development infrastructure rather than cultural amenity.

Data visualisation for B2B agencies – Bristol: A six-month data storytelling upskilling programme for 24 agency professionals in Bristol, funded through West of England Combined Authority, resulted in 18 participants taking on new client accounts within 12 months, generating an average of £45,000 in new annual revenue per participant. Programme cost: £180,000 total. The Bristol precedent is directly applicable to Aberdeen's advertising and marketing sub-sector, which has the client base (energy sector communicators) but not the data storytelling capability.

Engineering simulation to games/virtual production – Dundee: Abertay University's conversion pathway for engineers with simulation backgrounds into games development roles has produced over 60 successful career transitions since 2019. The pipeline from Aberdeen's simulation surplus into Abertay-supported games and virtual production roles is part of the rationale for the corridor bid.
Recommendation 2  Resolve the City/Shire structural fault line
Establish a Joint Creative Economy Board: the enabling governance condition for all other recommendations

title_page_text: Executive Summary
Background to the research

This research was commissioned by Aberdeen City Council to map the creative industries in Aberdeen and Aberdeenshire. The commissioners asked for a clear evidence base to inform the place of creative industries within the Regional Economic Strategy, support for future investment decisions, identification of opportunities for sector development, and practical recommendations for local authorities and regional partners. The research operates as both an economic mapping exercise and a strategic development study. It assesses the scale, composition and value of the creative economy; examines the relationships between creative, cultural, digital and energy-transition capabilities; and sets out actions for councils, regional agencies, funders, education providers and sector organisations.
What the data reveals and why this is different from national statistics

National statistics measure employment in registered businesses. Applied to North East Scotland's creative economy, that approach identifies just under 5,000 employees, including between 1,400 and 1,600  generic IT consultants. Self-employed and freelance practitioners do not appear in it at all. In a sector where over 90% of registered creative enterprises employ fewer than ten people and more than a third of practitioners are freelance, the exclusion of self-employed workers is a structural flaw in the measurement, not a small rounding error.

This research works across three layers of evidence: official administrative data from BRES and IDBR; real-time analysis of what companies are actually doing, derived from their website content, through The Data City platform; and LinkedIn workforce profiling, treated as a large-scale pre-filled occupational survey. The LinkedIn analysis identified more than 8,400 unique creative profiles among North East Scotland residents, including more than 1,500 additional employees and 3,280 self-employed and freelance workers not captured in official statistics.

The combined picture is substantially larger than any previous account of this economy. The region holds 10,490 creative workers, generating £453 million in direct GVA and £675 million in total economic impact. These figures are not visible in any current policy framework because the measurement tools previously applied were not designed to find them.

Between October 2025 and April 2026, the research team conducted interviews with stakeholders from policy, education, cultural and creative sector organisations, individual artists and support networks. Four in-person workshops in Aberdeen in November 2025 brought together practitioners, anchor organisations, local authority officers and representatives of national agencies.

The interviews and workshops arrived at the same conclusions as the desk research. The data showed a sector weighted towards freelance and micro-enterprise activity, lacking the deep commercial middle ground found in comparable regions. Workshop participants described the same view from the sector's perspective: the freelance tier is "hidden, hungry, struggling and undervalued" (AAMD_002). The fact that the two lines of evidence converge on the same structural conclusion gives confidence in both sets of findings.
What a comparison with the UK national picture and other areas highlights as the strengths of NES's creative economy
North East Scotland's creative economy has two structural characteristics that are unusual in the UK context and that are not the result of any regional or national creative economy policy.

The first is the nature and depth of its technical capability. The research found far higher levels of simulation, visualisation and engineering-grade digital skills in the regional workforce than those found in other UK regions. The industrial origin of these skills matters: they were generated and sustained by decades of safety-critical offshore operations, making them more deeply embedded and more resistant to displacement than capability built through any policy programme. They can be translated into markets for renewable energy as the oil and gas sector declines, and they open up new markets for immersive and real-time entertainment in film, games, live events and new kinds of visitor experience.

The second is the character of the rural and coastal cultural sector. Hundreds of independent artists, makers and musicians have built their own studio communities, open studio networks and retail platforms, generating real commercial output that official statistics miss entirely. This is a structural feature specific to a region with deep craft and cultural traditions embedded in dispersed rural and coastal communities. Creative economies of this type are rare in UK city-regions.
Both structural conditions create distinct commercial opportunities that a region without them cannot readily acquire. The strategies in this report exist to make that opportunity reachable.
What a comparison with the UK national picture and other areas highlights as the weaknesses of NES's creative economy

The distinctive structure that creates North East Scotland's strengths also contains a built-in limitation: two commercially valuable parts of the economy have developed in parallel without yet finding a way to work together.

There is a cohort of technical and engineering firms, many of them working in energy and adjacent sectors, that hold capabilities in simulation and 3D visualisation technologies that content, entertainment and communications markets would pay a premium for. The city-centre creative agencies hold creative strategy, storytelling and production capability that energy-domain and transition communications clients need. Each holds what the other needs to reach higher-value markets.

The skills the region lacks are precisely the bridging skills that would allow those two halves to connect: virtual production, data storytelling and real-time rendering (see Part 5.3 for detailed analysis). Their absence is measurable in both the quantitative and qualitative evidence and it is the direct consequence of the separation between the technical and creative economies.

Graduates leaving the region's universities with the technical and creative skills this region needs are more likely to pursue a career in other parts of Scotland, the rest of the UK and overseas because the distinctive career that combining creative practice with the region's simulation and visualisation skills could support has never been made clear to them at the point when they decide whether to stay or go. Closing the creative-digital gap could improve retention rates and, in the medium term, encourage more alumni currently working elsewhere to return.
What are the drivers of the resulting distinctive sector structure?

The sector currently contains three groups of people and organisations, each playing a distinct role. Cultural anchor institutions, including museums, galleries, performing arts venues and heritage bodies, sustain the public programming, skills pipeline and institutional credibility on which the rest of the sector depends. Commercial creative and digital SMEs generate the revenue, employment and supply chain connections that give the sector its economic weight. Rural and coastal artists, makers and musicians carry the distinctive character of the cultural offer. Doric language, fishing and farming tradition, and the visual and musical culture of the north-east coast give the region's creative work a character that external markets recognise as distinctively their own. That heritage spans four millennia and is still active in the work being made today.

Outside Aberdeen city centre, practitioners are spread across a wide rural and coastal area, with little physical or networking infrastructure to connect them. Because they are spread across such a wide area, those connections have never had the chance to form naturally. That is why investment in shared space, meeting and event facilities and mobile programming would return more here than in an economy where some of that already exists.

The research identified three opportunities for growth. The first is the convergence between creative practice and the technical skill base generated by 50 years of offshore energy. The per-capita concentration of simulation and visualisation skills in the workforce runs at 3.5 times the rate found in Nottingham, the most comparable UK city-region for this analysis, and we found nothing equivalent in any other comparable UK city-region we have studied. Those skills transfer directly into high-value screen, games, immersive and technical production, but the exchange of creative and technical knowledge that would make it happen has not yet developed. The second opportunity is cross-sector and interdisciplinary working, which the dispersed geography of the sector currently works against. The third is formal and informal networking to share knowledge, skills and access to domestic and export markets, which many practitioners currently lack. The strategies set out in this report address all three.
Are we double-counting digital sector activity in IT and software?
No; read together, this report and the earlier report from Opportunity North East into the Digital Tech sector clarify the relationship between the regional technology base and the creative economy.

title_page_text: ITQ Action Plan deliverable compliance matrix
Mapping the creative industries in North East Scotland: supporting document

title_page_text: Recommendation 1: Joint CoSTAR bid

Recommended vehicle: RGU as lead applicant, University of Aberdeen as academic co-applicant, both local authorities as public sector co-applicants, Scottish Enterprise and Opportunity North East as named partners. This mirrors the structure of successful Creative Clusters bids elsewhere. The bid should be developed by the academic partners in close consultation with the Joint Board once established; before that, a working group drawn from the Creative Industries Working Group should hold the development process.
Confirmation needed: whether RGU's research office has formally agreed to lead the bid, and whether the University of Aberdeen is willing to be a co-applicant rather than a parallel lead.
Recommendation 2: Joint Cultural and Creative Economy Board

Recommended vehicle: Joint committee of both councils for year one, using the Creative Industries Working Group as its operational base, with a commitment to review the legal structure after the first year of operation. The joint committee model provides the democratic authority and budget-holding capacity the Board needs without the delay of a new legal entity. The one full-time equivalent officer resource should be jointly funded from year one; without dedicated capacity, no governance structure will be effective regardless of its legal form.

Confirmation needed: whether both councils' legal and democratic services have confirmed that a joint committee with a shared budget line is achievable under current legislation, and what the minimum lead time for establishment would be.
Recommendation 3: Align creative economy with energy transition

Recommended vehicle: Joint Board as creative economy lead, ETZ as energy sector lead, ONE as economic development convener, with a formal programme agreement between the three. The four specific actions have different natural leads and should be assigned explicitly rather than held collectively.
Confirmation needed: whether ETZ and ONE have been consulted on their roles in this recommendation and whether both have expressed willingness to participate in a jointly governed programme.
Recommendation 4: Creative Ecology Structural Fund

Recommended vehicle: Joint Board as administering body, with both local authorities as joint funders and Creative Scotland as co-funder, where organisations are on the pathway to MYF eligibility. The ACC Catalyst Fund and the Aberdeenshire Council cultural support budget provide the initial capitalisation before a formal joint fund line is agreed. The structural fund should have an explicit exit condition rather than operating as a rolling subsidy.

Confirmation needed: whether both local authorities have confirmed in principle that a joint cultural fund with a shared budget line is achievable within current governance arrangements, and whether the Catalyst Fund can be directed toward this purpose.
Recommendation 5: Full-spectrum measurement (NES Culture Data Hub)

Recommended vehicle: Joint Board lead with Creative Scotland as data standards partner. Until the Joint Board is established, both local authorities should jointly commission the first iteration, with a commitment to transfer governance to the Board on establishment. The NES Culture Data Hub should be designed from the outset to feed into Creative Scotland's national data infrastructure to avoid creating a parallel system that requires separate maintenance.
Confirmation needed: whether Creative Scotland has expressed willingness to support a regional data hub of this kind, and whether the Culture Data Lab platform is technically suitable.

title_page_text: POLICY PLAYBOOK
North East Scotland Creative Industries Strategy
Five costed, sequenced and accountable recommendations
How to use this document
This Policy Playbook translates the five strategic recommendations of the main report into a programme management instrument. Each recommendation is presented with:
- The specific actions required (not just the intent)
- The lead body and delivery partners
- A costed range broken down by year
- A delivery timeline in 6–12–24-month bands
- Measurable KPIs against which progress can be reported
- Key risks and dependencies that could delay or prevent delivery

The Playbook is designed to be extracted from the main report and used as a standalone working document by the Joint Cultural and Creative Economy Board (Recommendation 2), by programme officers in both local authorities, and by Creative Scotland and Scottish Enterprise in their supporting roles. It is also the submission artefact requested by Scottish Government as evidence of a costed, actionable plan. The options appraisal underlying the selection of these five recommendations, including the pathways considered and set aside, is set out in Appendix D of the main report.
Recommendations are sequenced by strategic priority.
Recommendation 1 (CoSTAR bid) carries the firmest external deadline( the June 2026 Innovate UK call confirmation) and active bid preparation is required now.

Recommendation 4 (Creative Ecology Structural Fund) has the most urgent delivery window: some connective organisations are at immediate risk of dissolution and the window for intervention is measured in months, not years.
Recommendation 2 (governance) is the enabling condition for the others to function as a coherent programme.
Master delivery sequence
The table below shows the delivery timeline for all five recommendations across a four-year implementation horizon. Shading indicates when each recommendation is in active delivery.
Table 1  Master delivery sequence
Recommendation 1: Advance a joint CoSTAR bid
Strategy 1: Connect complementary capabilities commercially
Aberdeen–Dundee Creative Technology Corridor: positioning Aberdeen's simulation surplus for UKRI cluster investment
Rationale and opportunity

UKRI's CoSTAR (Convergent screen technologies and performance in realtime) programme represents the largest available UK investment in creative industries convergence. Aberdeen's typological differentiation – energy-creative convergence in an oil transition economy, with a simulation surplus at 3.5 times the per capita concentration of comparable UK city-regions – is a compelling case for CoSTAR cluster investment that Edinburgh, Glasgow, and London cannot replicate. Within the headline creative economy, the region has 920 Tier 2 registered creative businesses generating £226 million in direct Tier 2 GVA; around the headline creative economy sits a further pure adjacent tier of around 25 firms with confirmed creative-technical crossover activity, not included in headline BRES counts due to their classification outside the defined creative sector but identified in this report's convergence mapping, and around 90 Group B firms in the energy services and engineering sectors whose simulation and visualisation capabilities are directly contiguous with creative technology markets. This is precisely the evidence base a CoSTAR bid can deploy.

CoSTAR Realtime Lab (led by Abertay University), based at Water's Edge, Dundee, is a real-time virtual production R&D lab for games, film, animation and immersive media that combines game-engine, motion-capture and real-time graphics technologies to support industry-led R&D, prototyping and commercialisation in the creative tech sector. A satellite lab in Aberdeen would bring North East Scotland's outstanding capability and capacity in simulation and 3D visualisation, creating a corridor with the profile and diverse market demand to compete for investment at a scale that neither city could achieve individually.

A call for proposals for CoSTAR satellite labs is expected to be announced in June 2026; a bid must be in active preparation now. This is the recommendation with the largest potential financial return: a successful CoSTAR award of up to £5 million would fund the cluster development infrastructure, CPD programme delivery, and convergence firm connectivity programme that the strategies in Part Nine and recommendations in Part Ten of the main report require.
Table 2  Strategy 1: Connect complementary capabilities commercially
Case vignettes: Strategy 1 - comparable interventions

The School of Informatics at University of Edinburgh: This offers a direct precedent for pan-regional cooperation within CoSTAR. The School of Informatics is a core CoSTAR Realtime Lab partner supplying AI/ML and generative-AI research expertise, researchers (including postdocs), and data-analytics capability; it helps host the Edinburgh site (with Edinburgh College of Art/Design Informatics) and contributes to R&D in real-time graphics, content generation, motion capture/animation and production pipelines.

South of Scotland CreaTech Fund: The most directly comparable Scottish precedent, providing investment in creative technology businesses in a region transitioning from traditional industries. Early-stage firms receiving support showed average revenue growth of 34% in the first two years. The fund established the precedent of treating creative technology as economic development infrastructure rather than cultural amenity.
